words or compound words. 3.2. Suffixes forming adverbs, for example, -vat, etc.

Homage to Samantabhadra.
Even those who speak according to logic are defeated in debates by the deceitful through the presentation of fallacious arguments.
This [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of refuting that [view]:
"The statement of what is not a member of the proof and the failure to point out a fault constitute the points of defeat for both [the proponent and the opponent]."
But anything else is not tenable, and thus it is not accepted. //1//
The accomplishment of the desired object is the *sādhana* (proof);
its constituent part (*aṅga*) is that which brings it about; the non-statement of that part is the failure of the proponent to utter that constituent part.

The occasion for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consists in accepting that [position] and then remaining silent due to a lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), or because one is unable to provide a valid member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*).
Indeed, there are only three kinds of evidence that serve as the means for establishing what is not perceived:

essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Their validation consists in establishing their pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the probandum and then proving its presence in the subject (*dharmin*).
For example, whatever is existent or produced is all impermanent,
such as a pot and so forth.

Or, [the formulation] may be "sound is produced. Here too, there is no restriction regarding the sequence, because there is no difference between the two cases in terms of establishing the intended object. Having first established existence in the subject (dharmin), the pervasion (vyāpti) is subsequently established as well.
For example, sound is existent or produced;
and whatever is so, all that is impermanent.
"Just as a jar and so forth.
Here, the proof of pervasion consists in demonstrating a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case:
"If everything that exists, or whatever is produced, were not subject to momentary destruction..."

It would follow that for a non-momentary entity, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible through either succession or simultaneity, it would be excluded from the definition of being characterized by causal efficiency; thus, it would be simply non-existent. For that which is devoid of any description of capacity is defined as "non-designatable" (*nirupākhyam*).

Thus, when no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is presented against the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya-viparyaya*) for the means of proof (*sādhana*), there is an absence of contradiction; and even if its occurrence in the opposite case is not observed, the doubt—"it might be both produced (*kṛtaka*) and eternal (*nitya*)"—is simply not dispelled. Therefore...
Because there is doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it would be an inconclusive fallacy of the reason (*anaikāntika-hetvābhāsa*).
Nor can exclusion be established by mere non-perception, for one who does not see all things cannot perceive [the absence of the reason] in remote cases.
Because non-perception does not establish non-existence,
since even for those things that exist, some may not be perceived by one with limited vision.
Furthermore, the subverting proof is that wherein there is an impossibility of either succession or simultaneity;
for such [an entity] possesses no causal efficacy whatsoever.
And since that [non-momentariness] is impossible in what is non-momentary,
the [logical reason's] lack of capacity, as it functions, entails the definition of non-existence. Therefore, it is established that whatever is existent or produced is necessarily impermanent.
And by that much, there is the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) with the mere property of the probans (sādhana-dharma),
[which constitutes] a reason of essential identity (svabhāvahetu).
And the definition [of the reason] becomes established.

Here too, for one who does not accept non-perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established because the impossibility of [the cause acting] either successively or simultaneously is itself unproven; thus, the previous reason [also fails].

[Objection: There is no pervasion (avyāpti). If it is argued that here too, upon the commencement of the proof, there would be the consequence of infinite regress (anavasthā), [we reply: No, because non-perception (*adarśana*), which is the means of proving non-existence, is not prohibited. That non-perception which establishes the opposite of the reason when the opposite of the probandum is present—
Therefore, this is called a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) because it establishes the opposite [of the probandum].

For in this way, that reason would be established as being absent when the probandum is absent, provided that it were subverted therein by a [reason] possessing a means of valid cognition that is contradictory to itself. Otherwise, in that case...

In the absence of a subverting proof (bādhaka) for this [non-existence], doubt is difficult to dispel. Furthermore, the non-perception of everything does not constitute a subversion of an entity's existence. In that regard, it is established that causal capacity is pervaded by the application of either succession or simultaneity.
Because there is no other alternative, non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi) subverts the capacity for causal efficiency in that which is non-momentary;
for it is established that the impossibility of [acting] either successively or simultaneously is pervaded by the absence of capacity.
There is no consequence of infinite regress.

Thus, in the applications of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) reasons, the member of proof (*sādhana-aṅga*) is established. The failure to establish that [member] constitutes the non-statement of a member of proof for the proponent.

A point of defeat (*parājaya-sthāna*) arises because the intended object is not established; for even when a reason (*hetu*) that is factually capable is employed, its capacity is not demonstrated. Even in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), there must be a justification of the probative factor (*sādhana-aṅga*), which is the effect—
A mark (liṅga) is employed for the purpose of establishing a cause;
its relationship as cause and effect with that [cause] is established by means of two instruments of knowledge (pramāṇa): those that establish presence and absence.
Just as this comes to be when that exists— despite the presence of other capable causes for it— it does not come to be in its absence; in this way,
its status as an effect of that [cause] is established beyond doubt.
Otherwise, if one merely demonstrates that [the effect] does not occur in the absence of that [specific cause],
then even if another [cause] is absent there, the capacity of this [first cause] remains doubtful; for something else might be capable there.

In the absence of that [cause], it is not real. Furthermore, its cessation upon the cessation of this [cause] is a mere accidental coincidence, like being born in a region where one's mother’s marriage was customary.
Just as in other regions there is an absence of the date palm (*piṇḍakharjūra*) due to the absence of marriage with one's mother,
so too, when that [cause] is thus established, its respective effect is accomplished. This is established.

Existence establishes the occurrence of that [effect] through its own occurrence, because an effect does not deviate from its cause. And since there is no deviation, the same logical principle applies to all effects in relation to their own causes. Thus, the proof regarding the "reason of effect" (*kāryahetu*) is also not established.
The failure to state the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of that [reason] for one who asserts it is a ground for defeat (*parājaya-sthāna*),
because when those [parts] are not established, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not proven, since another object is not necessarily connected to its existence.

Because there is no necessity for the existence of an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) to entail the existence of that [effect], the intended object is not established; for even if a material cause (upādāna) exists, it does not necessarily indicate the effect in reality.
Furthermore, regarding non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), it applies only to that which has reached the conditions for apprehension (upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta) for the cognizer.
The proof by non-apprehension is the establishment [of the object],
because the conventional usage of "non-existent" is established precisely through such non-apprehension.
Because the non-existence of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility is not established merely by the cessation of perception by the cognizer, even though it is perceptible;
in that regard, reaching the conditions for perceptibility consists of a specific nature (*svabhāva*) and other causes.
And completeness [is established] by the specific nature [of the object], which is not remote through the three kinds of remoteness,
and which is distinguished from the appearance of the form of a non-self.

It has the nature of appearing in the direct perception of the perceiver. Such a thing, when other conditions for apprehension are present, is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent" because it is not perceived in that manner. Otherwise, if the logical mark (*liṅga*) were otherwise, there would be doubt.

In this case as well, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that everything of this kind is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent" (*asad-vyavahāra*), because if one accepts any non-existent thing, it does not differ from that [very] definition; for if such a thing were not accepted as being non-existent, its application [as non-existent] could not occur elsewhere.

For there is no non-perception of such an existing thing when other conditions for perception are present. This conventional usage of "non-existent" is based solely on the fact that such a thing, though not being perceived, does not exist.
Because no other cause for that exists.
If it is argued that the cause is the exclusion of all causal capacities (*sarva-sāmarthya-viveka*), [we reply:]...
Thus it is:
this cognition belongs only to one who distinguishes all causal capacities; for another, there is no such comprehension.
Because of the absence of a means [to establish it]. And when there is the apprehension of that [absence], the conventional usage of "non-existent" occurs;
this is said to be its cause.
The conventional usage of "existent" [arises] from cognition, designation, and causal efficacy; in the opposite case, [it is non-existent].
And if it is argued that there is the conventional usage of "non-existent," then there occurs the conventional usage of "existent" for a cognition possessing the aforementioned appearance.
In the opposite case, there is the conventional usage of "non-existent.
However, regarding that which is not an object of perception, there might arise from some source even for that which is produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*) the conventional usage of "existent.
But the conventional usage of "non-existent" in the opposite of that [perception] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because even when there is an absence of the perceiver's direct perception or of any other means of valid cognition regarding a remote object, doubt still persists.
Furthermore, not all cognitions and designations establish the existence of a real entity, nor its difference or non-difference,
nor the existence of the difference or non-difference of a real entity; for this is the case even with respect to things that are non-existent in some sense,
such as those past or future, or those that perform various or single causal functions.

To establish that state, even though there is an absence of a manifold or unitary self, there occurs a manifestation of manifold and unitary forms: King Mahāsammata was the progenitor of the royal lineage; Śaṅkha, the universal monarch, was the one who raised the sacrificial pillar constructed by Mahāsammata.
The horn of a hare,
visible form (rūpa) which is demonstrable and resistant,
and a jar— these words such as "demonstrable" and so forth do not have various distinct entities as their objects in a single [locus].
If it is argued that there is a synthesis (upasaṃhāra) in a single instance even when the objects are diverse, because those causes [of the cognition] are inherent (samavāya) therein;
Alas, this poor entity has fallen into labor;
having assisted many related things, it hopes for many words within itself from them.
By means of those various powers, it [assists] the many related things.
If [the object] assists by means of those very [qualities], why does it not produce multiple words?
For in this way, the labor of following a succession [of causes] is avoided;
otherwise, if there were an incapacity to produce multiple words, there would be no connection with multiple [relata].
Let there be no benefit [conferred];
for if there is no benefit, their connection to those [entities] is not established either.

Furthermore, let even the term "jar" refer to many things such as color and so forth, which perform a single purposeful action and are thus denoted by a single word; what is the use of postulating a separate entity?

For indeed, even many things may perform a single function, as in the case of the eye and other [senses]. We consider it logical that a single word might be applied there to establish their capacity for that [function]; moreover, people do not apply words to objects without a purpose.
In that regard, if a single word were employed to establish the existence of those objects— whether they function together or separately— which have a single purpose,
what would be the consequence? [The consequence would be] their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

For a collective term (*samudāya-śabda*) employed to establish a single capacity (*śakti*), there is indeed no contradiction with the singular number. Since that capacity belongs to the members joined together as one, rather than to each individually, the collective term refers to a single aggregate (*samudāya*) as its denotable object.

The singular number is used in the word "ghaṭa" (pot). Regarding words denoting a genus (*jāti*), since the capacity of the objects [denoted] exists both individually and collectively, there is both a manifold and a single capacity; thus, when there is the intention to express either a manifold or a single capacity—
The plural and the singular would occur according to one's wish— as "trees" or "tree"—
if there were this restriction that the plural must be used only for many things and the singular only for one. For us, however, [this applies] to conventional meanings, based on convention.
Therefore, the claim that "usage occurs due to [the speaker's] power" is precisely a form of dogmatic attachment (*anabhiniveśa*).

If it is argued that various individual forms such as color and so forth are capable of giving rise to a single word, then do objects themselves give rise to words independently of human usage? No, they do not.

Or rather, are words assigned by persons to objects for the sake of linguistic usage? For if they were to arise spontaneously, one might consider whether there is an inherent power or lack of power in the entity itself;
but that is not tenable. Since they are assigned by persons, [they can be used] according to their will.
If they were to enjoin [the agent], what fault would there be in that?
Furthermore, the cause for such an injunction has already been stated. Moreover, if color and the other qualities were not related to a single word, [the following would occur].
How can there be a connection with these [objects] by means of a single substance that is considered their substratum? This is merely an adherence to what is non-existent.
We do not deny the existence of a single word because of a contradiction in its having a single connection.

However, because there is a contradiction between the non-different forms of color and so forth and their performing various purposeful actions (arthakriyā) and being designated by various words in objects such as jars or blankets, those [forms] would not perform any purposeful action that is impossible for other collections [of causes]. Therefore, in order to manifest that [single effect], by means of each individual...
By the word "also" (api), it is not being said that this might be the desire of someone: "Let it be that form and the other [sensory objects] are of a single nature across all collections.
For what is this perception by direct sense-consciousness (*adhyakṣa-darśana*) that apprehends forms appearing as mutually distinct?
One disregards this [position]. And this is undesirable because it would entail a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the collection of form and the other [sensory objects].
If the pot were something entirely different from form and the rest, it would have to be a single entity.
What would be the consequence? Let it be so;

for that which is directly perceived, having as its nature formlessness and so forth, what obscuration could there be to its manifestation in its own nature within the intellect through its distinction from those [other factors]? It is manifesting.
Furthermore, objects are perceived distinctly even when they occupy the same location— as in the case of odor, taste, and so forth;
and even when they are apprehended by a single sense organ— as in the case of the touch of wind and sunlight.
Moreover, this indeed is the perceptuality of perception:
that its own nature is presented to the intellect through its distinction from the nature of non-self.
This jar, however, is one who buys without paying any price.

That which does not manifest its own nature yet desires to claim perceptibility— by this, cognition, sound, and so forth are also explained, if they are intended as the means of proving that [perceptibility]. And it is not...
If perception were not overpowered, there would be no non-perception of form,

by which a logical mark (*liṅga*) could be stated for its proof. Even if it were imperceptible, [there would be no basis for] the existence of that which is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Approaching [it] in that way is not logical. Therefore, a jar is not something other than its form and other such qualities.

Thus, for the time being, there is no conventional usage of "existence" based on cognition or designation, nor is there any conventional usage of the distinction or non-distinction of existence; for this very reason, there is no reversal [of these usages] through the reversal [of those factors].
However, from causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) there may arise the conventional usage of "existence," but not the conventional usage of the distinction or non-distinction of existence.

Because even a single thing is observed to perform multiple purposeful actions, such as a lamp’s producing consciousness, the modification of the wick, and the generation of a subsequent flame; and because even multiple things, such as the eyes and so forth, are observed to perform a single action, namely the production of a single cognition.
We do not say that there is a difference in existence merely because of a difference in causal efficiency;

rather, it is by means of a difference in unobserved causal efficiency. That causal efficiency which, having been unobserved in a certain thing, is subsequently observed, establishes a difference in existence.

Just as the capacity for causal efficiency, such as holding water, which is not perceived in clay, is seen in a jar; and although the capacity for causal efficiency, such as providing clothing, is not perceived in the threads, it is seen in the cloth— this is existence (*sattā*).
A distinction is established;
thus, a different object is proven, yet even so, the composite whole (avayavin) is not proven.
Just as in the continuum of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), a difference in causal efficacy arises due to the production of a difference in intrinsic nature according to specific conditions,
just as fire [arises] from the different stages of rubbing together the fire-drills (*araṇi*).

There is a difference in the capacity to burn coarse cow dung, grass, or wood. Likewise, because a difference in intrinsic nature arises according to the respective conditions, there is a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) among threads and other such things.
By this, the difference and non-difference of cognition and designation are explained.

In this regard, what was stated—that the establishment of the conventional usage of "existence" proceeds from causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and its opposite from the opposite—is true. However, that very opposite [non-existence] is not established in the case of those things that have reached the conditions for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). In that case, moreover, this [is the point]:
Even against one's will,
that which possesses this capacity— being present and meeting the conditions for perception— is not perceived.

Therefore, it is the object of the conventional designation "non-existent," because existence is characterized by causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*). Even so, what is the distinction of this [causal efficacy] from the previous [nature]?
For causal efficacy is not a separate entity from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); rather, it is that very [nature].
The non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension is itself the non-apprehension of its intrinsic nature;

thus, this is the same non-apprehension as the previous one. Therefore, by means of this non-apprehension, one who accepts the conventional designation of non-existence for certain things in certain places [must do so].
It must either be accepted or not accepted, since there is no distinction anywhere.
Since that [reason] is indistinguishable in other such cases as well, let it be so for them too; this is the pervasion (*vyāpti*):
everything of this kind, when unperceived, is the object of the conventional usage of non-existence (*asad-vyavahāra*).
If it is argued that even that which is not perceived anywhere, in any way, is nonetheless an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent," [we reply] no,
because everything would never cease from possessing all possible forms at all times.
Everything would be applicable everywhere and at all times; and this would not be the case:
that "this is from that," or "this is not from that."
This is here, this is not here; now this, now not this.
"This is thus" and "this is not thus"— because there is an absence of any cause for distinguishing any form whatsoever, in any manner, anywhere, or at any time.
The entire universe would lack positive concomitance and negative exclusion,
because there would be no differentiation.
If it is argued that "the systematic order [of things] arises from the differences in the cessation and occurrence of states," then— surely!

Those very [non-apprehensions] are not possible because of the absence of the conventional usage of non-existence regarding all objects, from which [usage] their systematic establishment might arise. If one accepts the conventional usage of non-existence with respect to some object, it must be stated why that is so; for it does not follow from mere non-apprehension.
There is no other cause for exclusion, because in the case of exclusion through both affirmation and negation, non-apprehension alone is always the means of proof. From non-apprehension...
If that is indeed accepted, one must state that wherever it exists, all conventional usage regarding non-existence (*asad-vyavahāra*) has that very thing as its object,
because there is no distinction [between them].
If it is argued that non-apprehension is the cessation of all means of valid cognition, and that where this occurs, its object is held to be non-existent,
then the "beloved of the gods" (devānāmpriya), being of tender intellect, does not tolerate [this].
01011 He did not pay heed to this because of the great difficulty involved in the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its conventional usage.
01012 For the non-occurrence of inference and the other [means of knowledge] does not lead to the cognition of non-existence, due to the possibility of error;
nor does the non-occurrence of all perception [lead to it], because such a case is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Nor is there a cessation of the non-differentiation from one's own perception regarding remote objects. Therefore, it is a specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) from which,
by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the conventional usage of existence (*sad-vyavahāra*) is invariably established.
The cessation of that [conceptualization] establishes the conventional usage of its non-existence,
because of the existence of its own nature.

Because [existence] is pervaded by the existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, for an object that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), there is no apprehension other than through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such that its apprehension would have to occur through inference (*anumāna*).
Nor is there non-perceptibility without a change in its nature (*tad-rūpa-anyathābhāva*).
And if there were a change into something else, that very thing would not exist.

Furthermore, from where has this sorcery— devoid of mantras or medicinal herbs— been learned by existence, such that it possesses no excellence of form that is unarisen or lost, and is neither obstructed nor distant?
These states belong to that very person, such as the sense faculties and so forth; they are sometimes perceptible and sometimes imperceptible,
by which means there is at times an inferential apprehension of them.
Sometimes perception [is the authority] and sometimes scripture;
for there is no superiority in this very matter, because these various modes are mutually contradictory.

It is not the case that there is no distinction [between entities], because the differentiation of conventional usage is admitted through the cessation of one excellence (*atiśaya*) and the arising of another excellence. Since that excellence is identical with its own nature (*ātmabhūta*), how could it not constitute a difference in essential nature (*svabhāva-nānātva*) when it ceases and when it arises, given that it is non-concomitant (*ananvaya*)?
It draws [them] forth like pleasure and pain. And if there is a causal continuity (*sānvayatva*), what activity or cessation could there be, and for whom? This is trivial.
Alternatively, if the activity and cessation of some intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were [to occur] spontaneously...
If those two [birth and destruction] are admitted [to be non-different from the entity],
why does the opponent not accept that very same thing?
If it is argued that this is because he accepts birth and destruction as being without any underlying continuity (*niranvaya*), then who...

This is what is called "continuity" (*anvaya*): the capacity of an entity for arising and perishing. That capacity indeed exists even prior to its birth and even after its cessation. Therefore, this entity does not arise as something entirely new in every respect.
"It does not perish first. If it is always devoid of any excellence (*atiśaya*), how is it that there is now this distinction in conventional usage based on something possessing excellence?
If you say that those states possess excellence, then [you must explain] those states and that [entity].

Regarding this capacity (*śakti*), is it a single entity or manifold? If it is one, how then can these [opposing qualities] exist simultaneously and without alternation within a single, undivided self, being mutually contradictory?
It will be joined [with the following]: birth and non-birth, cessation and non-cessation, unity and plurality,
perceptibility and imperceptibility, utility for causal efficacy and lack of utility, and so forth.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because "state" (*avasthā*) and "capacity" (*śakti*) are synonymous terms, then the "Beloved of the Gods," being prone to forgetfulness, fails to perceive the context. This contradiction was stated on the premise that capacity and state are one and the same entity, without distinction.
Now, if there is no distinction between these two and no contradiction whatsoever,
it would not be the case that the birth and destruction of an entity merely possess a continuity (*anvaya*), because that which has continuity...
There is neither birth nor destruction for that which has neither; nor is there continuity for that which lacks these two.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of the non-difference between them, alas, this is no answer at all!
01208 This is a perilous situation arising from defects.

Your Honor, even while being led astray by a passion for [mere] appearances, does not perceive himself [as such]. For that which is called "non-difference" is indeed unity; and those two [terms] are based upon difference.

How can conventional discourse regarding existence be applied? [For instance,] how are such things as non-cessation and non-manifestation during cessation and manifestation, or stability and instability, which constitute the characteristic of diversity, to be joined [to reality]? For this indeed is the differentiation of entities, and the absence thereof is non-differentiation.
Just as [the qualities] such as pleasure and so forth, as well as power and state, reside in a single self; otherwise,
because there would be an absence of the defining characteristics of difference and non-difference, there would be no determination of difference and non-difference anywhere.
The manifestation [of something] within its own self is non-difference;
in the opposite case, there is difference, just as a jar manifesting within the nature of clay is non-different from it.

If it is argued that there is a distinction between pleasure and pain in their opposites, and that this constitutes the definition of distinction and non-distinction, and therefore there is no contradiction;
Indeed, the manifestation of the jar does not occur within the nature of the clay;
rather, it is a certain [manifestation] that has the very nature of the clay itself.

A jar [is not one]. For there is no single entity consisting of clay throughout the three worlds, because there is a distinction in the appearances of individual cognitions and a distinction in the intrinsic natures of the substances. For in this way, even for this [clay], regarding pleasure and so forth...
And the comprehension of difference among conscious entities is possible only if such difference actually exists;
yet, even while this [difference] is present, there is oneness due to the continuity (anvaya) of some aspect of the self.

If [you argue that it is so], then this same consequence would apply to pleasure and the like, as well as to conscious entities. Furthermore, there is no inherence in its entirety even in the case of jars and such, because that would entail the consequences of a lack of diversity and simultaneous origination.
Moreover, no one perceives a jar and its clay-nature as distinct from one another.
By means of which it might be known that "this has appeared here. For such a thing does not occur when the locus and the occupant of the locus cannot be perceived as distinct.
Nor is there an appearance of a power within the essence of the power itself; therefore, [it cannot appear] within its own self.
There would be no non-difference. By this, transformation (*pariṇāma*) is also refuted; for even one who might imagine that [the effect] belongs to [the cause],...

Transformation is non-different from that [substance], for there is no transformation of the self of a power; furthermore, what is meant by this term "transformation"? It refers to the modification of that which remains persistently present.

The transformation of a substance consists in the cessation of one attribute and the manifestation of another attribute; that which is the attribute ceasing and that which is the attribute manifesting— this is transformation.
Is that [entity] the very same substance that remained [previously], or is it a different object? For there is no other conceptual alternative.
If it were that very same [substance],...

Since its persistence involves neither cessation nor manifestation, it must be stated for what these two [cessation and manifestation] belong to. Furthermore, it is not established that they are "other attributes" (*dharmāntara*) of that which persists;
for that very thing cannot be both itself and something distinct from it, independent and devoid of dependence.
It becomes a different property (*dharma*).
Now, if the property (*dharma*) were a distinct entity from the substance (*dravya*),
then its cessation—

There is no transformation of a substance through disappearance and appearance. For a substance cannot undergo transformation through the disappearance and appearance of things that are distinct from it;
otherwise, this would absurdly entail the same for consciousness as well.
Furthermore, the designation "the property of a substance" would not be established due to the absence of a relationship;
for there exists no real relationship between entities other than that of cause and effect.
And yet, there is no relationship of cause and effect between these two.
Because that which is not of the nature of [the substance] itself cannot have it as its cause,
since a property (dharma) is an entity distinct from the substance (dravya).

Even if it is a different entity, because it produces another property as its effect by being the cause of that property, the transformation of the substance would be accepted; and that is not contradictory even for something else.

In the continuum of cause and effect, which is designated as the substance "clay," when the subsequent effect— the substance "pot"— arises from the preceding causal substance— the lump of clay— it is accepted that the conventional expression "the substance clay has undergone transformation" applies.
Furthermore, no other conceptual alternative is possible for a dharma apart from its identity with or difference from the substance;
in either case, there is no transformation.
A phenomenon is not the substance itself devoid of distinction,
nor is it a separate entity from the substance.
Rather,
it is the arrangement of a substance that constitutes a different state,
just as a fist is [the arrangement] of fingers. For a fist is not merely the fingers themselves without distinction.
Because extended things lack the nature of a fist,
nor are they something other [than the parts], by virtue of having a separate intrinsic nature.
If it is argued that [the fist] is not perceived, we say no;
for the fist is a particular state of the fingers.
Indeed, certain fingers themselves constitute the fist.
Not all [fingers]. For fingers extended [in a fist] do not possess a nature devoid of distinction from the fingers in the fist;
[the distinction exists] in both states.

Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of admitting] a real entity (*pratipatti-prasaṅgāt*). For indeed, that very distinction which is inherent in the nature [of things] is the defining characteristic of the differentiation of entities, just like pleasure and pain. And if the arising of distinction were something extrinsic (*parabhūta*), then the fingers would be perceived only as being extended; for it is not the case that...
For that which does not itself deviate from its own nature, there would be a perception of it as otherwise upon the arising of a different entity,
because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
But was it not said that the state is neither the substance itself nor something distinct from it?
"That it is a different entity from substance"— this has been stated,
but it is not logical;
for regarding an existing thing, no other mode is possible apart from its being either identical to or different from [another].
In those two cases, because their characteristics exist through mutual exclusion regarding the object,
the abandonment of one is invariably concomitant with the adoption of the other. However, in the case of the fingers,
which perish moment by moment, those that are extended are simply different [fingers].
The fist is something else.
In that regard, words such as "fist" refer to specific particulars,
whereas the word "finger" refers to the universal.
It is the object [of cognition], like the words "seed," "sprout," and so forth, and like the word "rice" and so forth. Therefore, when the fingers are extended, they do not constitute a fist.
Thus, if the effect were non-existent in the cause beforehand, why would it not [arise]?
Everything arises from everything, for there is no distinction whatsoever in that which is non-existent.

But surely, even if everything exists everywhere, this same fault applies; for there is no distinction whatsoever in that which exists. Or, if there were such a distinction, that distinction would arise from the three *guṇas*.

It would have to be distinct [from its cause], because in the absence of that [cause], the particularity [of the effect] would not persist. Furthermore, since it already exists in its entirety, what could possibly be produced at the stage when it is fully accomplished? Thus, the means of production would be rendered futile.
Furthermore, since there is no specific thing to be proven, if some kind of excellence were to arise there from something that was in some way non-existent,
then that excellence would be non-existent there.
How is it produced? Or, if it were produced, the same objection would apply: everything could be produced from everything.
It is not the case that there is no excellence whatsoever in that [cause], for [the effect] arises only from that which already exists in some way.
If this is argued, [we reply: since that mode by which it does not exist is itself non-existent there, how could it arise?
Furthermore, it has been stated that for that which exists in every respect, there can be no purpose for its arising.
Even if an effect were to arise from a non-existent cause,
that which has the nature of producing a particular thing would produce that very thing from itself.
The restriction "not from anything else" applies to that as well;
its own nature-restriction arises from its own cause, and thus the restriction of the nature of entities is beginningless.
Furthermore, if the pot exists within the lump of clay,
why is it not perceived in that state as it is later?

Or [it is] its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). If it is argued that this is because the manifestation (*vyakti*) has not yet appeared, [we reply: since that very thing possesses the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) when that causal efficiency and so forth exist, and since that form did not exist previously.

How can a jar exist? For when one form exists, another form does not [simultaneously] exist. Nor is it logical that there be no difference in the entity despite a difference in the appearance of forms.
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, that which possesses a nature meeting the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) but is not perceived simply does not exist. For there can be no non-perception of something while its own nature remains present.

And its non-abiding is non-reality, just like the mutual non-abiding of suffering and pleasure; thus there is a pervasion [of the reason] by the certainty of the conventional designation of "non-existent" through the specific non-apprehension [of the object].
Therefore, by one who establishes the exclusion of something through non-apprehension,

its fulfillment of the aforementioned definition of apprehension must be demonstrated. Having demonstrated this, the statement of non-apprehension constitutes the formal justification in the case of the non-apprehension of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

In the case of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) as well, the establishment of the absence of the pervader is the "justification" (*samarthana*), after having first established the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the two properties.
In the case of the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) as well, [the justification consists in establishing] the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

Establishing the cessation of a cause after having established [the probandum] is "corroboration" (*samarthana*). In the case of the perceptions of contradictories as well, the demonstration of one of two contradictories as being contradictory [to the probandum] is "corroboration."
Thus, in the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the failure to justify the member of the proof (*sādhana-aṅga*) constitutes the non-statement of a member of the proof;
that is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent when there is a failure to justify it.
Because [the reason] is unestablished with respect to that [subject].

Alternatively, it is called a *sādhana* (means of proof) because by means of it, an object not previously known to others is established; thus, the *sādhana* is the collection of statements consisting of the three-fold reason. Its constituent part (*aṅga*) is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
The term "and so forth" refers to this. The failure to state even one of these [three members] constitutes the non-statement of a member of the proof (*asādhana-aṅga-vacana*).

This too is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent, because if that [member] is not stated, there is an absence of proof due to the non-statement of the very form of the reason (*hetu*).
Alternatively, it is the inclusion within a proof-statement of that which is not a member of that very proof— namely, the proposition (*pratijñā*), the application (*upanaya*),
the conclusion (*nigamana*), and so forth—
which constitutes the non-member of the proof.
This is a point of defeat for the proponent,
because it is a futile statement.
Or [it is so] regarding the positive and negative concomitances in the case of similarity or dissimilarity.
And since the proof is established by the statement of only one [member] of the syllogistic application,
the second is ineffective; thus, the statement of that which is not a member of the proof is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) precisely because it is a useless statement.

But is it not the case that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) must indeed be presented, even if it is not a constituent part of the proof, for the purpose of indicating the object [of inference]? No;
because it is redundant. Even in the absence of the proposition—
In the statement, since the establishment of the intended object occurs precisely from the aforementioned proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*),
its inclusion is useless. Furthermore, if there were no arising of cognition without the presentation of the subject matter (*viṣaya*), [then its inclusion would be necessary].

How is it that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not a member of the proof (*sādhana*)? For there is no purpose of the proof other than being the cause for cognition, which applies equally to the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth as it does to the statement of the thesis. Thus, the thesis-statement is also [a member of the proof].
[Objection: How is it not a means of proof (*sādhana*)? [Reply:

If you argue that it is not a means of proof because the mere [statement] lacks capacity, then that applies equally to the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) as well; therefore, even that would not be a member of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*).
For the cognition [of the probandum] does not arise from the mere statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) alone.
By this, the arising of doubt is also refuted,
even from the statement of the property of the subject.
Because doubt arises from a mere [reason] when the relationship [between the reason and the probandum] has not been demonstrated,

therefore the inclusion of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) in the proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*) by the proponent is indeed useless and constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Alternatively, that which is not a constituent part of the establishment of the proof— namely, a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), or the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)— its statement by the proponent is also a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because it constitutes the employment of what is incapable [of proving the thesis].

Likewise, the statement of a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*)— such as one that lacks the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and so forth, or one that fails to demonstrate positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) or has unshown concomitance (*apradarśitānvaya*)— is also a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent,
because it is merely the employment of what is incapable [of proving the point], for there is no connection between those [fallacies] and the logical reason (*hetu*).
It cannot be demonstrated;
because it is not demonstrated, it lacks capacity.
Alternatively, "accomplishment" (siddhi) means proof (sādhana); it refers to that purpose which has such a factor as its constituent part.
The basis of the dispute, which is the cause for initiating the debate, is a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*).
Apart from that, there is no other specific [point] based on a treatise (*śāstra*) that is not intended to be known.

The insertion of fallacies (*vyāja*) and so forth, as well as making a proclamation, for the purpose of deluding the opponent, obstructing their power of response, and the like— that too is the proponent’s point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), consisting in the statement of what is not a constituent part of the proof (*asādhana-aṅga-vacana*).
Because it expresses something irrelevant,
and because the meaning accompanied by such a qualification is not what the opponent desires to know; however, there is no fault if there is a desire to know it.
Furthermore, when another matter that was intended to be investigated arises through a succession of incidental digressions—
such as [discussing] the fallacies (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) and so forth— among the external opponents, the adjudicators,
and those who perceive the logic, they must simply bring the debate to an end; they must not [allow it to continue].
For no matter what the purpose may be, nothing whatsoever is employed when it would lead to an undesirable consequence;
however, for one who propounds selflessness, even dancing, singing, and so forth would follow as an undesirable consequence in that context.
For example, someone might proceed by first stating a proposition:
"We Buddhists say that there is no self. Who are the Buddhists?
Those who have accepted the teaching of the Blessed Buddha. Who is the Blessed Buddha?
"In whose teaching did the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa go forth? Who, again, was the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa? He for whom there is a drama named *Rāṣṭrapāla*.
Having raised the question, 'What kind of drama is this *Rāṣṭrapāla*?'—"
At the end of the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra* shall then enter, recite, dance, and sing. Since the opponent would be unable to imitate that entire performance, he would be defeated.
01918 This is the manner of investigating reality among the learned who are esteemed by the assembly (sabhyas).
01919 But in this way, a conclusion for the matter at hand is not possible; since it results in a lack of certainty, the debate would not even be commenced.
And how is there victory and defeat in this way?
Even for the opponent, there is the same kind of consequence regarding non-reiteration;
thus, the reiteration [of the argument] must be stated in detail.

Because it arises through a pretext and because it is uncertain, the mere statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not even logically justified. How much less, then, can there be the introduction of an irrelevant discussion regarding uninvestigated particulars, or the false prattle resulting from the attempt to explain that [thesis]?

Moreover, this entire category [of arguments] has been propounded by the wicked and dishonest, who are incapable of establishing a meaning through the power of logic. For example, having made the proposition that the body, the instruments, the world, and so forth, are preceded by a preeminent Person (puruṣātiśaya),...
Under the guise of explaining the body, the sense organs, and the world, he proclaimed the entire meaning of the Vaiśeṣika scriptures;
and in the debate as to whether sound is eternal or non-eternal, [he refuted] the reality asserted by Jaimini, the author of the treatise that elucidates the expansion of the twelve characteristics.

Having formulated the proposition (pratijñā): "A pot is accompanied by something other than either [the word] 'pot' or the locus of permanence," there follows an exposition of the meaning of the twelve characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
All of this is merely a means for the concealment of the incapacity of those of dull intellect; it is not, however, [the truth].
It is endowed with the truths because,
upon the investigation of reality, recourse to results and so forth, as well as the application of punishment and so forth, are inappropriate.

If it is argued that in the case of announcing a drama (*nāṭaka*) and so forth, there is defeat because one has shifted to another meaning, then why would this not also apply to anything else that was not intended to be known? For even in that other case, there is no necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) with the establishment of the intended property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*).

Just as impermanence is not established without establishing the suffering of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and so forth, which are characterized by dependence upon causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-pāratantrya*),
such [impermanence] is—
Even though the property (*dharma*) has not been stated separately, because it is included within the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), it is indeed made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*);
therefore, there is no separate presentation or explanation of it.
Consequently, even for such an object that is not currently desired to be known by the opponent at that time—

Whether it occurs within the thesis (*pratijñā*) or elsewhere, introducing or explaining something other than the intended meaning constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because it leads to a different subject matter. Therefore, only the specific property (*dharma*) sought to be known should be stated as a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*); one should not introduce an incidental digression (*prasaṅga*).
Because if that were admitted, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Thus, when the opponent has demonstrated that the proponent’s statement of a non-essential element of the proof constitutes a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna), [the proponent is defeated].
Otherwise, there would be neither victory nor defeat for either of the two.
The failure to point out a fault [in the argument] is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the respondent (*prativādin*). By the proponent (*vādin*), [the fault must be pointed out].

When a proof has been employed, if the opponent— who has accepted the position of the respondent— does not point out a defect regarding the subject matter at that time, he should be declared defeated. Furthermore,
the defects of a proof are deficiency, unestablishedness, and inconclusiveness.
The proof of the opposite of the point intended to be established by the proponent,
as well as the eighteen faults of the example— failing to point these out, failing to make them known,
and failing to explain them, constitutes the ground for the defeat of the opponent.
Furthermore, that [defeat] occurs because the proof is faultless,
or even if it is faulty, because the opponent is unaware of it or lacks the capacity to demonstrate it; for when a faulty proof is stated, [the opponent does not incur defeat].
Furthermore, it is not logical to establish the defeat of either the proponent or the opponent when a fault has not been demonstrated,
since their defeat consists precisely in the mutual impairment of their respective capacities.

The determination of victory and defeat is made in relation [to the opponent]. Since there is no true understanding from a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), there is indeed no victory even for one who fails to provide proof. For in the investigation of reality (*tattvacintā*), there is no practice of quibbling (*chala*).
If this is so, why is there no defeat?
Because of the loss of the establishment of reality (*tattva*).
It is not [a case of defeat] because there has been no refutation. For defeat by another occurs only through the refutation of that [position], not otherwise.
There is no absence of proof, because the absence of proof does not depend upon a counter-positive;
for even when the means of proof is absent, the absence of proof exists even in the absence of a counter-positive. And as for the counter-positive...
Because there is an inability to refute that [position], there is no defeat; thus, there is no defeat.
Therefore, even though this person has stated an ineffective proof, he must be declared undefeated so long as the opponent has not demonstrated its such [ineffectiveness].

If it is argued that even debate involving quibbles (*chala*) is a discussion among those seeking victory, we say no; for the engagement of the virtuous in the treatises occurs within the context of countering the misconceptions of the wicked. Indeed, those engaged in benefiting others do not undertake false prattle for the sake of self-exaltation or the disparagement of others.
They teach such improper conventions. Furthermore, it is not the conduct of the virtuous to acquire gain, honor, and fame by disparaging others;
nor is it for those esteemed by the virtuous to cause suffering to living beings by giving with their own hands to those who act in such a manner.

It is appropriate for the authors of treatises and the members of an assembly [to engage in debate]. Furthermore, the treatises on logic (*nyāya*) are not composed by the virtuous for the sake of acquiring gain and the like. Therefore, there is no such thing as "debate for victory" (*vijigīṣu-vāda*) that is prescribed by the rules of yoga; rather, the virtuous are engaged in the activity of benefiting others.
In order to instruct one who has fallen into error, they should follow the path of logic by either stating a valid proof or by pointing out a real defect,
in the presence of witnesses.
It is for the sake of awakening to that very [truth]. That very pursuit of logic is the discourse of the virtuous;
if one who seeks the reality of things should understand it through the stated logic, then—should there be no such understanding—[the following applies].
If it is argued that even another person might not understand [the truth],
and therefore those seeking victory must employ quibbles (*chala*) and the like in order to protect the truth, we say no.

It should be stated that this applies even to [acts such as] scratching with the nails, slapping with the palms, striking with weapons, or setting fire [to one's own body]. Therefore, this is not a superior means for protecting the truth; rather, the proclamation of the proof (*sādhana*) is the means for the virtuous to protect the truth.
And there is the semblance of proof (*sādhana-ābhāsa*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*);
for in their absence, even if one inflicts injury upon another through false chatter, the reality [of the matter] is not established. Otherwise, [it would be] logic (*nyāya*).
Because it is established by the wise as being for the purpose of exposition; therefore, the victory of the proponent consists in the revelation of reality for the sake of favoring others,
whereas [the defeat of the opponent] consists in the perception of actual faults through [the exposure of] falsehood.
The withdrawal of the opponent's position;
or, that which is not a fault of the proof, because even when it exists, there is no obstruction to the establishment of the point intended to be proven by the proponent.
The pointing out of that [defect] by the opponent is a ground for defeat, because it constitutes the statement of a false rejoinder.

Just as a property (*dharma*) that is not intended by the proponent as something to be proven (*sādhya*) may nonetheless be considered "to be proven" because it is accepted in a treatise (*śāstra*), the pointing out of a contradiction (*virodha*) occurs by means of the reverse of that [acceptance]. It does not exist [otherwise].
"The self" constitutes the pointing out of a flaw in the thesis (*pratijñā-doṣa*), namely that there is a contradiction between your [proponent's] thesis and its constituent terms.

"Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately after effort" [is an example where] the reason (*hetu*) is a part of the meaning of the thesis, because it is a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*) of the subject.
Pointing out what is unestablished (*asiddha-udbhāvana*),

and pointing out defects such as all the futile rejoinders (*jāti-uttara*) beginning with "balancing the similarity" (*sādharmya-sama*) and "balancing the dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya-sama*)— this is called "pointing out what is not a defect" (*adoṣa-udbhāvana*).
When the proponent has demonstrated that what was [alleged] by the opponent is merely a fallacy (*doṣābhāsa*), the opponent must be declared defeated,

because the proof in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is faultless. However, when the proof is indeed faulty, there is neither victory nor defeat for either of the two parties, because of the [lack of] reality—

Because of the failure to proclaim [one's own position] and because of the failure to expose the opponent's faults, and because victory occurs only when the establishment of one's own position has been accomplished without a counter-position,
therefore, one who desires to win must establish their own position and refute the position of the opponent.

It must be refuted. Even when the proponent has stated a flawless proof, if a fallacious objection (*doṣābhāsa*) is raised by the opponent, [the proponent] must simply demonstrate that it is a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsatva*).
Victory and defeat [occur] in this way,
and not otherwise,
even when the truth is stated according to its actual nature, provided there is no counter-position.
Because there is no capacity to manifest reality through refutation; nor does it apply even to the opponent here, because their misconception is [only] false in a real sense.
This definition of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been stated by us as being logical;
however, that which is otherwise is not tenable and is therefore not accepted.
For that [case] wherein this aforementioned definition of the points of defeat does not exist—

We have not stated that it is improper for this to be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Having refuted the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya regarding the statement, "The abandonment of one's own proposition (*pratijñāhāni*)— which consists in admitting the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) into one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*)— is a point of defeat," the author of the Vārttika [proceeds as follows].
This [opponent] states the "position of the established" (*sthita-pakṣa*). We say that very thing:

when one admits that a property belonging to the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) exists in one's own example (*sva-dṛṣṭānta*), he should be known as defeated (*nigṛhīta*). In that case, it is both seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and at the end (*ante*).

"Established" refers to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). One's own example is one's own position (*svapakṣa*), while the counter-example is the opposing position (*pratipakṣa*). [The proponent attributes] the property of the opposing position to their own position.
By granting [the opponent's point], one is defeated;

for example, when one says, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the proponent of the counter-position objects on the basis of the universal (sāmānya), [the original speaker] says:

If it is argued that "if the universal is perceptible by the senses and eternal, then let sound be likewise," this constitutes an abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), because of the relinquishing of the previously asserted impermanence of sound.

In this regard, since there is an abandonment of the accepted thesis, there is a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*). What determines the specific restriction [of the fault] when one abandons the thesis in this manner?
For it is possible that the exposure of a fault in the reason (*hetudoṣodbhāvana*) might occur by another way as well.

By stating the proof of the counter-position through [the words] "beginning with" (ādinā) and so forth, there is both the abandonment of one's own position and the acceptance of the opponent's position. And this very thing is the primary cause for the loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*); thus, by what has been demonstrated in this way, the thesis must be abandoned.
"And in the case of [the opponent's] abandonment [of the position], there is defeat.
But this [objection], namely, "If it is said that 'the universal is eternal and perceptible by the senses,' then let sound also be so," is entirely irrelevant. What person of sound mind would...
One who asserts that "sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," while merely pointing to a general example, would thereby understand sound to be permanent;
for even though the universal (sāmānya) is permanent, it is observed to be perceptible by the senses in the case of the impermanent jar.
One would be in a state of doubt.
If it is argued that one might nevertheless understand it due to dullness,
even so, what is the point of demonstrating the universal?
In the same way, it should be stated that sound is eternal, because there is no investigation regarding the understanding of an insentient entity;
nor is it the case that when its property is understood in sound by means of the demonstration of an eternal universal, [the object is thereby established].
One becomes authorized to employ a counter-argument; for one who says "sound is impermanent," the direct counter-argument would be "sound is permanent," not "the universal is permanent."

Therefore, because the property of being perceptible (*aindriyakatva*) occurs in both the eternal and non-eternal positions and thus deviates from the probandum, its employment as something that is not a constituent part of the proof constitutes a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*),
and not [the mere presence of] a counter-position.

By this method, there is a loss of the proposition (*pratijñā-hāni*) due to the admission of a property (*dharma-anujñā*). When the meaning of the proposition is negated, the specification of that meaning through an alternative property (*dharma-vikalpa*) constitutes a "different proposition" (*pratijñā-antara*). For example: [The original proposition is] "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses."
Thus, when a refutation has been made by demonstrating the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of that reason,

[the opponent] formulates another proposition (*pratijñāntara*) by means of a conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*) regarding the properties of the universal (*sāmānya*) and the pot (*ghaṭa*), specifically through the distinction between the properties of being omnipresent (*sarvagatatva*) and non-omnipresent (*asarvagatatva*), as follows:
"A jar is non-omnipresent and impermanent; likewise, sound is also non-omnipresent and impermanent.

This is called the point of defeat known as "a different proposition" (*pratijñāntara*), because even when the capacity of the proof is present, there is a failure to understand it. For he [the proponent], having previously stated "sound is impermanent,"...

In order to prove his own proposition, he states the subsequent proposition: "Sound is not omnipresent. He says that the explanation of its meaning is for the purpose of demonstrating that [proposition]. Its meaning is the statement of the subsequent proposition for the sake of establishing the previously stated probandum; that is the meaning of the term "its meaning" (*tad-artha*).
This is the explanation. Furthermore, since one proposition is not capable of proving another proposition, this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Even here, by speaking in this manner, one does not [present] a new proposition for the sake of proving the previous proposition.
What is meant is this:

when the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has been raised against the reason (*hetu*) of "being perceptible by the senses" (*aindriyakatva*) on the grounds that it occurs in a universal (*sāmānya*), [the qualification] "non-omnipresence" (*asarvagatatva*) [is introduced].

When the qualification "being perceptible by the senses" (*aindriyakatva*) is applied to the reason (*hetu*), he avoids the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); however, he does not state a different proposition (*pratijñā*),
namely that [the object] is non-omnipresent (*asarvagatatva*).
Because [the probandum] is already established in the word, and because a thesis is characterized by the indication of that which is yet to be proven.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that one states a subsequent thesis in order to prove a prior thesis—that too is incorrect; for a thesis does not serve to prove another thesis.

If it were stated [in that way], it would become a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*); rather, it is the indication of the means of proof (*sādhana-nirdeśa*), because it is employed for the sake of establishing what is to be proven (*sādhya*) through any one of the [three] members beginning with the reason (*hetu*).

It would not be a statement of the probandum (*sādhya*). Since the characteristic of a reason (*hetu*), namely its similarity to the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*), exists in the case of non-pervasiveness (*asarvagatva*), whereas the characteristic of a proposition (*pratijñā*) does not, the application of "reason-hood" to non-pervasiveness does not constitute a separate proposition. Absolutely—
And this is incoherent, for he states the proposition (*pratijñā*) in order to prove that very proposition.

For one who, having first stated the proposition, knows how to state the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), and so forth, certainly knows some sequence of the proof; and knowing it, [he would not speak thus].

How could one whose internal organ (antahkarana) is unimpaired employ the very thesis for the sake of proving that thesis? And by so employing it, he would be asserting that proof is achieved through the mere thesis alone.
And consequently, one should not state the reason even beforehand;
for it is impossible to enumerate such irrelevant matters of this kind.
Furthermore, the restriction regarding the definition is entirely irrelevant to the statement of a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*);
for "stating a different proposition" is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) precisely because it constitutes an irrelevant statement. This applies to all such cases.

Only a single definition would need to be stated. Furthermore, no such legal dispute has ever been observed before in which an effort is made for that purpose. Nor does a treatise proceed by following the idle chatter of children.

Furthermore, what would be the finality of their engagement [in debate], since they do not accept [the opponent's position]? Moreover, it is observed that even for the learned, there is no statement of something unestablished (*asiddha*) unless it has been thoroughly examined; therefore, based on the observation of such conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), a ground for defeat (*parājaya-adhikaraṇa*) of that kind is established.
Therefore, even in this case, if the opponent should point out the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) when the proponent has already ceased his expectation [for further proof],
it is because he has stated an inconclusive reason that is not a constituent part of the proof (*asādhana-aṅga*).
This is a point of defeat for the proponent;
likewise, if the opponent is unable to establish by means of valid cognition that the universal is real, perceptible by the senses, and eternal, [it is a point of defeat].

One might be able [to do so]. However, since there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the scriptural assertions made without specific reference, if these matters are not established by such a means of knowledge, the pointing out of actual defects is not possible;
thus, there is no defeat merely by virtue of an assertion, because the reality of the object is not thereby established.
Because the opponent has not pointed out a fault, and because he has stated a proof that is not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he does not even become a victor. However,
when the proponent further desires [to prove] impermanence, there is no fault whatsoever in his stating a qualification.
Because it begins with the justification of the reason (*hetu*).

Contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*). For example: the proposition that "substance is distinct from its qualities."
The reason "because no object distinct from form and the rest is perceived" constitutes a contradiction between the thesis and the reason. By this very [point],
a contradiction with the thesis is also stated in cases where the thesis is contradicted by its own words.
It is contradictory,
as for example: "a female ascetic is pregnant," or "the self does not exist"— [such is the nature of] the reason (hetu).

Contradiction (*virodha*) also occurs where the reason (*hetu*) is contradicted by the thesis (*pratijñā*), as in: "Everything is distinct, because the term 'existent' is applied to a collection. By this [the contradiction] with the thesis [is explained].

The contradiction with the example (*dṛṣṭānta-virodha*) has also been explained. Furthermore, contradictions of the reason (*hetu*) with the example and so forth, as well as contradictions with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-virodha*), must be stated regarding both the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason.

[This is because] one might urge that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the presence of] "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, which are established for oneself, within the opponent's position.
Contradiction (*virodha*) is that which demonstrates the deviation of the opponent's position by means of its own established [property], such as "cowness" (*gotva*).
This reply should be understood as contradictory when it is independent of one's own position;
likewise, it applies to one who employs a reason (*hetu*) that is independent of one's own position.

"In the argument 'Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses,' [the reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it contradicts the impermanence of *gotva* (cowness) and so forth, which are established for itself; it is admitted by both parties."
But [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika),
because the objection of inconclusiveness is based on a thing that is admitted by both parties.

In this case as well, since the employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) within the proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*) has been prohibited, there can be no contradiction between the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) based upon it or produced by it; thus, what is called "contradiction with the proposition" is not at all a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
It might be argued that even in the absence of the formal employment of a proposition (*pratijñā*), a contradiction between the proposition and the reason (*hetu*) is still understood,
as for example: "There is no perception of an object distinct from color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities]."
Even when it is stated that "that [substance] is distinct from its qualities,
and no substance is perceived as an entity separate from form and the other [sensory objects]," the probandum is indeed understood.
There is a contradiction between the two means of proof;
how, then, can there be the non-perception of another object and its exclusion from that [object]?

True, this contradiction would indeed arise if the reason were to establish the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*). For if [the reason] were [to function] by virtue of having reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāptatvena*)...
When a substance is present, its own manifestation is not perceived apart from the manifestation of [its qualities] such as form;
therefore, it is accepted that it does not exist apart from those [qualities]. This is the exclusion of the desired [object].
Since we have indeed stated that a reason which proves the opposite is a contradictory (*viruddha*) reason, this constitutes a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) if such a thesis—

A contradiction between the thesis and the reason is intended [only when the object is perceptible]. However, if its attainment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpti*) is denied,
then there is no contradiction whatsoever between the thesis and the reason.

Even for entities that are distinct [from the subject], although they are not perceived as distinct from it because they are remote from some point, their distinction nonetheless exists. As it was said: "When there is a contradiction with one's own words, there is a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñā-virodha*)."

Thus, in this case, the very basis for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is the employment of a thesis (*pratijñā*)— which is not a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*)— within the statement of the proof;
it is not a contradiction (*virodha*).

Because it has that as its locus. If contradiction were independent of the thesis (*pratijñā*), it would be a basis for defeat. However, since the thesis is the locus, defeat belongs to him solely because of the employment of that [thesis], given that the introduction and conclusion have reached their end. It is therefore useless.

Pointing out a contradiction [after the conclusion has already been reached] is like attempting to ignite what has already been reduced to ashes, because there is no further defeat for one who has already been defeated.
However, when several reasons are stated for a single probandum during the course of an investigation, [this is not a fault].
Their capacity for activity toward the accomplishment of that [result] through conceptual construction exists because otherwise the second [instance] would be redundant.
For if even there, the application of one could not occur without the application of the other, [the second would be useless].

At that time, there is no purpose whatsoever in establishing the second [proposition], because there is no need to demonstrate what has already been understood. Therefore, so-called "contradiction with one's own words" is not at all a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) regarding the thesis (*pratijñā*).

Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the thesis in the statement "the self does not exist," because what is being negated is that the referent of the word "self" has existence as its substrate. For a contradiction would arise only if the referent of the word were being negated; however, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the referent of a word.

Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding a contradiction of the reason (*hetu-virodha*) due to sublation by the thesis (*pratijñā*), such as: "Everything is discrete, because the term 'entity' is applied to a collection," in this case there is no employment of a formal thesis.
Nor is it because of a logical reason (*hetu*) by which there would be a contradiction; rather,
this is a concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra-vacana*) made for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning already established.
Having established by other reasons that a word does not denote a single particular,

but rather denotes a universal common to multiple objects, [the author] demonstrates that every word-meaning, by virtue of its manifold nature, lacks the existence of a singular, specific entity as its intrinsic nature.
Demonstrating the meaning of the word, one should state that "everything is distinct. By this, the contradiction with that [position] is refuted. And this is an illustration by example, as in:
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced and impermanent," for instance. In some cases...

Having demonstrated the use of words for a well-known general property (*sāmānya*) that encompasses multiple objects despite there being disagreement regarding the specific referent, and having thus established the point of contention, he concludes by way of generality: "Everything is distinct."
If it is asked: "Why has the formal application of the example not been stated in its direct order, and why has the object of dispute not been shown?"— it is not so,
because of the concise presentation.
Even so, because this is seen as a mere formal application (*prayoga*) and because it lacks the character of a proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*),

for this very reason there is no sublation of the reason (*hetu*) by the thesis (*pratijñā*). Nor is there anyone who, while asserting that "nothing at all exists," [intends to] express that [non-existence] as a collection (*samuccaya*).
One desires a single aggregate so that there might be contradiction [with the opponent's position].

Even for one who asserts the diversity of the atom through such statements as "because of its simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms]," it is not possible to establish a single entity in the form of an aggregate.
It is not accepted; rather, it is precisely a non-entity because of the negation of both unity and plurality.
Therefore, even that [collection] is not accepted as a "whole" (samūha), and since the word does not apply to it, there is no contradiction.

This contradiction does not differ from the previously mentioned contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), such that it would be stated separately. If it is argued that there is a difference because in the former case there is a sublation of the reason by the proposition, whereas here there is a sublation of the reason by the proposition;

For when there is a contradiction between the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*), there would be a relationship of sublated and sublator. Since every contradiction of meaning occurs between two [terms], they are mutually sublatory when another [term] is present in the same context.
Because there is no difference in meaning [between them]. In that case, there is no distinction in meaning between the separate refutations of the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*).
