Furthermore, whether this [reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*) or non-contradictory (*aviruddha*), when the reason is employed, it is irrelevant because it belongs to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*).
"Unestablished" (*asiddha*) refers to the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetu*), which is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Indeed, that [reason], being stated while perceived as not possessing the property of the subject (*atad-dharmatā*), brings about the speaker's defeat. Once he is defeated, there is no further consideration of contradictions regarding its meaning.
Moreover,
this contradiction between the thesis and the reason, occurring in all cases,
does not exceed two classes of fallacies regarding the reason: namely, being contradictory (*viruddhatā*) or being unestablished (*asiddhatā*).

And thus: contradiction [occurs] because, when the presence of the reason in the subject is established, it exists only in the opposite of the property to be proven, thereby contradicting the meaning of the proposition. Furthermore, non-establishment occurs when the two contradictory natures are not established in the subject as the meaning intended by the proposition.
Because [the two properties] cannot coexist in one [locus]. Nor is there a contradiction otherwise.

If it is argued that a contradiction is possible because of a contradiction between the meanings of the reason (*hetu*) and the proposition (*pratijñā*) when the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is unestablished;

But when there is doubt regarding both [the presence and absence] in the subject (*dharmī*) due to the application of an invalid means of knowledge, since the existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject is thus doubtful,
this is indeed the fallacy of the reason known as "unestablished" (*asiddha*); therefore, it is distinct from the "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

Contradiction with one's own thesis (*pratijñā-virodha*) is not indeed a ground for defeat (*parājaya-hetu*). Since "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and "contradictory" (*viruddha*) have already been mentioned by the very statement of fallacious reasons (*hetv-ābhāsa*), contradiction with the thesis need not be stated separately.

If it is argued that because contradiction depends on both [the thesis and the reason], either one may be specified according to the speaker's intention— namely, that there is a "contradiction between the thesis and the reason" (pratijñā-hetu-virodha) based upon both the thesis and the reason, and that this contradiction has both as its locus— it may be so; however, when the contradiction with the thesis is intended [to be expressed].

Then it is called a contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñā-virodha*); when there is a contradiction between the thesis and the reason (*hetu*), then the reason is "contradictory" (*viruddha*). Therefore, [there is] contradiction of the thesis and contradiction of the reason.

Or rather, there is no fault; for example, the reason (*hetu*) therein is "sound is eternal because it possesses the property of being produced," while the contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñā-virodha*) is "the self does not exist."

Examples of mutual contradiction between the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) include such cases as "sound is distinct from its qualities" and so forth; an example of contradiction between the thesis and the reason includes such statements as "there is no single entity."

No; for a contradiction that depends upon a reason does not transcend the category of a fallacious reason (*hetv-ābhāsa*), as was stated previously. Furthermore, when a contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñā-virodha*) is intended to be expressed independently and by itself, the inclusion of the term "reason" (*hetu*) serves to indicate that it is a "contradiction between the thesis and the reason."

This is incoherent. Furthermore, the charge of "contradiction of the reason" (*hetu-virodha*) is not tenable here even with respect to the statement, "It is not eternal because it possesses the property of arising," for [a contradiction of the reason] occurs when the reason is sublated by the thesis (*pratijñā*).

In that case, it would be a contradiction of the reason (*hetu-virodha*). However, here the proposition (*pratijñā*) is sublated by the reason; therefore, a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñā-virodha*) is appropriate. Even when a contradiction relies on both [the reason and the proposition], the designation of that specific contradiction is established based on the intention to indicate that which is being sublated.

As for what was also said— that by this [same logic], contradictions with the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and so forth regarding the thesis (*pratijñā*) should also be stated according to the maxim of a "clown's painting"— in that case too, there would be a contradiction if the example possesses the opposite of the property (*dharma*) that has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*). And when the example is contradictory...

If the occurrence of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is established as being non-common (*ananyasādhāraṇā*), then that reason is the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*). If it is common (*sādhāraṇā*), or if its restriction to that occurrence is not established, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); or, if it does not occur [in the subject], it is the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) fallacy.

If it is argued that when the contradictory instance is absent and the opposite is present, there is no fault in the reason (*hetu*) nor any contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñā*) by the instance, we say no;
for even that does not escape being a cause for doubt, since the contradiction of the instance indeed undermines the thesis.
The fault lies in the case of similarity (sādharmya), not in the case of dissimilarity (vaidharmya), because the latter is intended [as the proof].

Furthermore, in a case where the example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) possesses contrary properties, even if the reason (*hetu*) does not in fact deviate from the probandum (*sādhya*), its non-deviating nature cannot be demonstrated. Thus, there can be no certainty [of the probandum] from a reason that is not connected through a demonstrated inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*).
Therefore, the contradiction of the example with the thesis does not fall outside the category of fallacious reasons (*hetv-ābhāsa*).
If it is argued that there is a fault in both cases, we say no; for the fault of the reason has already been addressed previously.

Because one who has been defeated by means of a *prasaṅga* need not consider any other fault; specifically, for one who maintains that there is a fixed order for the members of a proof (*sādhana*), it was previously stated that the definition of a reason (*hetu*)— namely, similarity to the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*)—
is impossible in the case of a contradictory example.

Defeat occurs due to a fault in the reason (*hetu*) that has been employed; therefore, a contradiction based on the expectation of a subsequent example (*uttara-dṛṣṭānta*) does not deserve consideration. For even in the case of a reason, if there were a presence [of the reason] in a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*), it would result in either being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) or "contradictory" (*viruddha*) when there is a contradiction with the example.
However, when there is a contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
such as "fire is not hot because it is cold," this is indeed the fallacious reason known as the unestablished (*asiddha*).
The contradiction of a thesis with valid cognition has been explained by way of its contradiction with one's own words.
All these contradictions of the means of proof are included within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Thus, they are already stated by the very mention of "fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*).

As for the objection that a contradictory response (*viruddha*) regarding the opponent's position is a charge of "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntika*) based on [the reason] being established for oneself through [examples such as] "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth—

That is entirely irrelevant. For if he were to require the establishment of a deviation by means of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, which are established for himself, then that would be contrary to his own position and not what he intends; thus there is a contradiction.

It would be appropriate [to say this]. For he, being himself uncertain regarding the occurrence of the reason once the nature of "cowness" (gotva) has been apprehended, thereby manifests his own lack of comprehension. And that reason, whether cowness actually exists or not, has its capacity to prove [the probandum] unestablished, because it is a cause for doubt.

But once the capacity [of the reason] has been established as being indeed non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to "cowness" (*gotva*) due to its non-occurrence there, there is no longer any doubt; for this is because the proof has eliminated all possible modes of doubt. By this, [the fallacy of] employing a reason that is independent of one's own position is [also addressed].
The inconclusiveness has been explained;

he too, by asserting that the reason— which resides in the eternal "cowness" (gotva) as conceived by himself— is for the sake of [proving] non-eternality, fails because the member of the proof has not been established.
He states precisely the cause of doubt. Furthermore, regarding what was said— that there is an objection of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) based on an entity admitted by both parties—
there too, it is necessarily...

The inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason must be stated precisely by way of its being a cause for doubt. Since that [cause] is equally present when the [reason] is not established in other cases as well, there is no distinction between what is established for both parties and what is otherwise in terms of their being inconclusive.
As for what was also said—
that because they are preceded by fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*),
they are already included by the mention of those [latter] and thus are not stated separately among the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)— [that is incorrect].
That too is incorrect for one who maintains that there are other constituent parts [of the syllogism]. For one who asserts that the example is a separate constituent part from the reason,
it is not by the mention of a "pseudo-reason" (hetv-ābhāsa) that the "pseudo-example" (dṛṣṭānta-ābhāsa) is addressed.

The statement [of the reason] is the pervader, because that which is understood through its expression is [implied]; therefore, it follows that there is no need for a separate means of proof (*sādhana*). Since fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) are included within fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), it is intended that the example itself is also included within the reason.

And thus, the example would not be a separate member of the proof, because it does not function separately. Since the matter to be proven by the example is already included within the reason (*hetu*), it is established by the reason alone; therefore, the example has no separate efficacy whatsoever.

Moreover, there is no point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) that is logically applicable to the proponent of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣavādin) which does not involve some form of fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa); thus, all those [points] related to it are already expressed by the mention of the fallacious reasons themselves, and need not be stated separately.
They may occur; for even a reason such as "shifting to another matter" is possible only when the reason is indeed incapable [of proving the point].

Indeed, no one would begin to shift to another matter once the reason is capable and the probandum is established, because shifting to another matter occurs only when a person acts falsely due to incapacity.
03807 Withdrawal of the proposition (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*) is the removal of the meaning of what was proposed when the thesis is refuted.

03808 For example, one who has proposed the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses" [is said to withdraw the proposition] by demonstrating the deviation of the reason through its occurrence in universals (*sāmānya*). 03809 [End of fragment].
When a refutation has been made, if one abandons the position by saying, "Who said that sound is impermanent?",
this is the point of defeat called "renunciation of the thesis" (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*).
In this case as well, if he does not [defend] the thesis even when the fallacy of the reason (*hetu-vyabhicāra*) has been pointed out, [then it is a defeat].

If one abandons it, why would it not be accepted? If you say, "It is indeed defeated because of the statement of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)," then what is the point now of waiting for the abandonment of the counter-proposition (*uttarapratijñāsāṃnyāsa*)?
That itself is his first point of defeat; what is the use of other futile prattle and feeble efforts that cannot be definitively determined?
For if such things were introduced, it would lead to an infinite regress. This is especially true in the case of one who remains silent when their own thesis is refuted.

One might as well have to state that "remaining silent" is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for one who flees, or that "having fled" is a point of defeat; therefore, this [argument] is also incoherent.
When a reason has been stated without qualification and it has been refuted, the statement of another reason by one who desires to provide a qualification is "another reason" (*hetvantara*).
For example: "This manifest world has a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*), because it possesses magnitude (*parimāṇa*); [just as] things such as jars, which are preceded by clay..."

"The measurement of things such as shallow bowls is observed. To this, he objects by way of an exception: "The measurement of things of various origins and things of a single origin is also observed. Having been thus objected, he says:

Because we observe that modifications which possess a single primordial nature (prakṛti) have finite dimensions, all this manifest world, being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, is perceived as finite. Since it lacks composition with the form of any other primordial nature, it must consist of a single [nature].

[The opponent says: "It is due to its being of the same nature. This constitutes a different reason (*hetvantara*) when the opponent states a qualification after the previously stated reason has been refuted because it was stated without qualification.
And since there is the occurrence of a different reason, the previous reason lacks proving power; therefore, it is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

In this case as well, since the very same previous reason has been stated to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), what is the use of considering another reason once one has been defeated? If the proponent of the initial proof has already stated an inconclusive reason and has been granted the opportunity for a reply, [then the debate is concluded].
He is defeated by that very [point],
having no opportunity for a reply;
even if he states another reason, there is no defeat.
It is fit [to be called a "point of defeat"] because it does not cease [from the relevant discussion].
A "point of diversion" (*arthāntara*) is a statement whose meaning is unrelated to the subject at hand.
This occurs when, while the thesis and counter-thesis have been formulated according to the stated definition and the proof of the probandum is being attempted through a logical reason—
In the context of *prakṛti* (the base form), one might state: "Sound is eternal because it is intangible"—this is the logical reason (*hetu*).

Now, a "reason" (*hetu*) is a word (*pada*) ending in a *kṛt* suffix, derived from the verbal root *hi* with the suffix *tu*. And having introduced that a "word" (*pada*) consists of nouns, verbs, prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*), [the discussion proceeds].
He explains that [the opponent] provides definitions for the name and so forth; this "naming another matter" (*nāmāntara*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*),
because it is inconsistent with the meaning previously accepted.
This is a logical point of defeat (nigrahasthāna):

when a fault has been pointed out by either the proponent or the opponent in the preceding or subsequent position, to abandon the subject at hand and state something that is not a constituent part of the proof.
And [the defeat called] "failing to point out a fault" (*adoṣodbhāvana*). For when the proponent of the proof must provide a justification for the proof he has put forward,
failing to do so and instead stating something else— whether relevant or irrelevant, even if it is not invariably concomitant with the subject— is a ground for defeat.
The position [of the opponent] is that even for the respondent, there is the introduction of another [point] merely by pointing out a fault.
This is meaningless, like a mere enumeration of phonemes; for example: "Sound is eternal..."

"Because of the presence of *ja*, *ba*, *ga*, *ḍa*, *da*, and *śa*, there are *jha*, *bha*, *ña*, *gha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, and *ṣa*. [The opponent replies: "He is defeated because of the failure to state the proof (*sādhana*).
This too is irrelevant.

For it is not the case that there is pointlessness merely because the desired object is established from the instruction of the sequence of syllables; rather, whatever is the statement of that which is not a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*), that alone is pointless, whereas [that which is] useful for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not.
Because there is no subject matter and because it serves no purpose,
the inclusion of specific modes is irrelevant.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of the father’s appropriation [of the son],
this might be so,
like the instruction of the sequence of phonemes.
If it is argued that the suffix *-vat* is employed here [in the definition of *pratijñāntara*] and thus there is no fault because it may sometimes grasp something inappropriate, we say no;
for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of not mentioning other points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), such as shifting the subject (*arthāntara*).
For in this way, those [examples] need not be stated separately, because stating them would be purposeless.
That which is "purposeless" (nirarthaka) is not so called merely because it fails to establish the probandum; rather, it is that for which [the probandum] is simply not established at all.
If it is argued that some meaning exists and that [the statement] is therefore accepted as not being meaningless, then [it applies] to whatever that may be.
For even one who does not speak would be subject to defeat if he utters something meaningless, since there is no distinction in the grounds for defeat.
If it is argued that this is not so because such a case is not relevant here:

Whoever utters what is meaningless here, he is defeated by that very act. This applies equally to everyone who speaks what is not a constituent part of a proof; all such speakers of the meaningless are refuted by this very [rule].
One who is liable for defeat is defeated by means of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Furthermore, the mere recitation of the sequence of phonemes is not entirely useless; for in certain contexts, even that is meaningful. Therefore, it is only in this specific case that it is devoid of meaning.
[It would follow that] this [repetition] would be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Moreover, it is far too narrow to say that "the mere indication of a sequence of phonemes" is a point of defeat;
for [this definition would exclude] such cases as "chattering of the jaws" (*kapola-vādita*) or "striking the flanks" (*kakṣa-ghaṭṭitaka*), and so forth.
Or rather, it is because it is [something] to be expressed.

An "unintelligible meaning" (*avijñātārtha*) is a statement that, even though it has been uttered three times by the proponent, is not understood by either the assembly or the opponent. That is, a statement which has been uttered three times by the proponent and [is not grasped] by the assembly and the opponent.
When [an utterance] is not understood due to such causes as the use of ambiguous words, the employment of unfamiliar expressions, or being pronounced too rapidly,
that is "of unknown meaning" (avijñātārtha).

A point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) employed to conceal one's lack of capacity is not distinct from the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*); for if that [latter] were connected to the subject matter at hand...
One should indeed make [the argument] intelligible;
it does not lack capacity.
In that case, if the audience and others do not understand due to their own dullness, the learned person is not subject to defeat.
If it is argued that one who is worthy [of defeat] is indeed subject to defeat on account of their speech alone, without considering the wisdom of the assembly,
then why is the opponent not defeated for failing to understand what was stated by the proponent of logic due to his own dullness?

If, due to dullness, one lacks the capacity to explain what is not understood by the assembly and others, one would not be the victor, nor would one be subject to defeat. Since speaking incoherently is simply the "irrelevant" (nirarthaka) fallacy, there is no separate ground for defeat called "the unintelligible meaning" (avijñātārtha).

That which lacks a connected meaning due to the absence of a logical sequence between preceding and succeeding parts is "meaningless" (*apārthaka*). Where there is no connection between several words or sentences through a sequential relationship, its lack of coherence is apprehended.
Because the meaning of the whole is lost, that is "meaningless" (apārthaka),
like the sentence beginning with "ten pomegranates" (daśa-dāḍima).

This [category of *apārthaka*], it is said, is stated separately from *asambaddha-varṇa* (meaningless phonemes) because of the lack of connection between words; but surely, in that case, *asambaddha-vākya* (incoherent sentences) should also be stated separately. No, for *apārthaka* includes both.

Because it would follow that even what is meaningless would be included [in the category of defeat]. Furthermore, by resorting to such a distinction, you have already stated the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that results from propounding separate definitions for the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Nor do we perceive any fault whatsoever in the presentation of this inclusive description.
Or, to claim that there is some other quality in the distinction [of the members] is trivial.

A statement with the members inverted is "out-of-order" (*aprāptakāla*). The sequence of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the other members follows their respective definitions according to the requirements of the meaning.
In that regard, the statement of the members [of the syllogism] in reverse order is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
If it is argued that this is not so, because the proof is still established even in that case:
It is not so, because it is equivalent to a word that lacks actual usage.

For example, when the word *goṇī* is employed in the sense of the word *gauḥ*, it conveys the object possessing a hump and other such features; however, this is not an etymological derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the word.
It is useless, because by this word one understands the word "cow" itself, and from the word "cow," one understands the object possessing the hump and so forth;
likewise [it is useless] for the thesis and so on.
One grasps the sequence through the inversion of the members, and the meaning through that sequence; for instance, first the object (*karman*) is taken up, and after that the instrument (*karaṇa*).

"A lump of clay and so forth is the world"—this is like describing one madman to another; it is a statement devoid of logical application, as if [one were speaking] from the word "goṇī" (a sack) regarding that which possesses a hump and other such features. If [it refers to] that which has a hump and so forth...
There is no comprehension of the meaning;

we do not perceive the meaning through the effort of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of words, because the word *goṇī* lacks the capacity to convey the meaning. Since it does not convey [the meaning], [it is not a word].
If it is argued that the grammatical explanation is for the sake of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), [we reply:
surely, even from the word *goṇī*, comprehension is observed in common usage. [The opponent says: True, it is observed.
But it was stated that this is not direct [perception].
This has been stated, yet it is not logical, because for women and Śūdras there is the cognition of both.

Because of the absence [of that knowledge]. Indeed, only one who knows both the correct word (*śabda*) and the corrupt word (*apaśabda*) understands it in this way. But one who knows only the word *nakka* or the word *mukka*, and not the word *nāsā*—

How could he understand the meaning from that [word] after first understanding the word from a corrupt form? Furthermore, since comprehension is observed even in those who do not know both [the correct and the corrupt forms],
comprehension does not occur through a traditional lineage.
Furthermore, that which is incapable with respect to the meaning is also incapable of generating a cognition with respect to the word itself.

For even in the case of the meaning, what is called "denotative power" is nothing other than the generation of a cognition having that [meaning] as its object. And if an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) were to generate a cognition regarding the word itself, it would [generate it] only with respect to the meaning.
Why would it not produce [the cognition]? For we do not perceive any danger to this [person] from the object by which he would avoid it;
and because even with respect to a word for which no convention has been made, there is no production of cognition. For indeed...

This corrupt word (*apaśabda*) produces comprehension even regarding a [correct] word by its very nature, because it is not observed [to do so]; however, it could only produce it through convention (*samaya*). Why then does it not function toward the actual object itself by virtue of convention? For in this way, there would be an infinite regress of comprehension.
Exertion is thereby avoided.

Furthermore, because of the observation of the opposite: in the world, people are seen who, failing to comprehend the meaning from correct words, are instead frequently educated through corrupt forms alone.
Thus, the instruction on words (śabdānuśāsana) is useless.
If it is argued that it is not useless because its purpose is the derivation of refined (saṃskṛta) words, [we ask]:
what is this "refinement" (saṃskāra) of words? For they do not possess wisdom, physical strength, or extensive learning.
We perceive the initial formative impression (saṃskāra),
yet these [sounds] do not possess absolute audibility, nor is there any excellence in their capacity to convey meaning. No.
The status of being a means to merit (*dharma-sādhanatā*) is not established, because demerit (*adharma*) arises even from refined actions when they are enjoined as wrong conduct,
and merit arises even from other [actions] when the opposite occurs.
The proclamation that one attains the joy of heaven solely through the correct employment of words is a mere statement.

Those who understand reasoning do not respect such scriptures, nor [do they rely on] the mere correct employment of words devoid of any injunction regarding the means for accomplishing dharma, such as generosity and the like.
The mouth of anyone who says "falling into hell" becomes distorted.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a word called "refined" (*saṃskṛta*).
If it is argued that "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) consists in the usage by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), [we reply:]...

Who are the learned? They are those endowed with qualities such as having known all that is to be known. But what is this groundless persistence of theirs, independent of the excellence of their qualities, that they employ only these very words?
Nor [do we rely] on others. Furthermore, there is no witness here who is beyond the reach of the word,
by virtue of whom we might determine this in such a way.
Indeed, the learned do employ [such forms]. But in this case, not perceiving any excellence of quality (*guṇātiśaya*), how can we accept the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of certain words?
Or rather, there would be no effort toward its grammatical exposition, due to the absence of any excellence in its qualities;
furthermore, for one who does not abide by that tradition, the preservation of the Veda and so forth would be entirely purposeless.
Even though there may be an excellence of qualities, no effort should be made toward grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*),
because that inherent nature is established through other means as well,
such as Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa.

It is like the Draviḍa, Andhra, and other dialects. For there is no specific grammatical definition for the languages of each individual region; nevertheless, by virtue of traditional usage, people [understand them].
"In that very way one proceeds, and through the corruption of their usage,
there will be comprehension of those Sanskrit words. This engagement with the grammatical definitions of words is indeed the activity of the dull-witted.
Even if the order of the members [of the syllogism] is reversed, if there is still comprehension of the connection between those statements,
there is neither a reversal [of the meaning] nor a failure to comprehend the sense, due to the inherent capacity [of the words]. For in this matter,
there is no convention that the members must be employed in this very order, even though there is no difference in the resulting communication.
Thus,
that very sequence is such that the cognition of the object arises from the [phonemes] as they are situated;
there is no cognition from a reversal [of the order].

If it is argued that there is comprehension through the sequential order [of the sounds], we say no; for there is no comprehension of a sequential order from those [sounds] whose relationship is not being perceived.
Only in the case of those words for which some relationship arises does this [comprehension] occur here.
Since they are connected, once the relationship between them is known, what prior or subsequent order could there be among them by which they might be established? As for the relationship—

In the case of comprehension, that very sequence is theirs which is perceived as the relationship of the words as they are situated; for there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of words within sentences.
Some [hold that] it is like "the king's man" or "the man of the king. To the extent that a complete meaning is achieved by a certain number of words, that is a single sentence; for example:

"Devadatta, bring the black cow. In this case, even though the words may be employed in whatever order one desires, there is no difference in the comprehension of the meaning; thus, there is no insistence on a specific sequence.
And it has been established that [the meaning] is understood according to its actual state even without the explicit statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

If it were argued that "cognition will arise," then there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the employment of a word whose meaning is already being cognized. Furthermore, after demonstrating the relationship in the remaining cases,
the presence [of the reason] in the subject (*dharmin*) should be demonstrated.

There is no fixed rule that the relationship must be demonstrated only after demonstrating the presence [of the reason] in the subject (*dharmī*); for it has been stated that comprehension arises in both ways. Furthermore, this applies even to words whose relationships are not explicitly perceived.
Since there is no comprehension even from those [words] taken in succession, this [fallacy] does not differ from the "irrelevant" (*apārthaka*); thus,
the "untimely" (*aprāptakāla*) should not be mentioned as a separate category.

A statement is deficient if it lacks even one of its constituent members. That statement in which any one of the members—such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth—is absent is deficient; for in the absence of the means of proof (*sādhana*), the probandum (*sādhya*) cannot be established.

"It is not deficient in its thesis (pratijñā-nyūna) that is 'defeated' (hīna), because even in the absence of those [additional words], the cognition [of the meaning] occurs"—this has been established. Another [teacher] says: "That is indeed defeated even when there is deficiency, because one who employs a word that is meaningless despite the meaning being already understood [is defeated]."

He would deserve defeat. To say that [the thesis] is not the proponent of what is connected with the goal (*artha*) is an unconsidered statement. For this very reason, the thesis does not possess the status of being a member of the proof (*sādhana*).

The "redundant" (*adhika*) occurs when there is an excess of either the reason (*hetu*) or the example (*udāharaṇa*). Since the purpose is accomplished by one, the other becomes useless; this should be understood as applying when a restriction (*niyama*) has been accepted.
This refers to cases where an investigation is preceded by the employment of a single statement of proof (*sādhana-vākya*).
In that context, stating more than is required is a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because it is purposeless; however, in a discursive debate (*prapañca-kathā*),
there is no such fault, as there is no restrictive rule.
Repetition of word and meaning is "redundancy" (*punarukta*), except in the case of restatement (*anuvāda*).
Repetition of the word is, for example: "Sound is impermanent; sound is impermanent. Repetition of the meaning is, for example: "Sound is impermanent; it is of a nature to cease; it is a resonance."
Thus [it is said].

Here, verbal tautology (*śabda-punarukta*) need not be mentioned separately, because it is already included within the discussion of semantic tautology (*artha-punarukta*); for when there is a difference in meaning, even if the words are identical, [there is no fault].
There is no fault [in this], as for example: "When the master laughs, she laughs; when he cries out loudly, she cries out excessively;
when he girds his loins, she runs after him with a burst of sweat."
He reviles and censures that which is endowed with virtues and free from faults;
yet a machine purchased for a mere fragment of wealth dances and performs its dance. //2//
Or, for example, when something exists, another thing exists; when it does not exist, that other thing does not exist—
then the latter is the effect of the former.

The other [type] is the cause (*kāraṇa*). Furthermore, even a restatement of a meaning already understood is a tautology (*punarukta*) when used in a formal argumentative statement (*sādhana-vākya*) where the specific wording is fixed, such as the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā-vacana*).
Since its meaning is already covered by the repetition of the sense (*artha-punarukta*), it need not be mentioned separately.
Furthermore, this [defect] should be stated as a fault only in a syllogism with fixed means of proof (*niyata-sādhana-vākya*), and not in an elaborate discourse (*vistara-kathā*).
For one who is explaining [the teaching], fearing that there might be incorrect hearing or understanding, may say [the same thing] again and again to witnesses and others; yet even so, in that case—
If it is argued that there is some deception because [the teacher] is not the object [of the instruction], we say no;
for it is not the case that "this one is the teacher and this one is not the student," and thus it is not through effort [that the distinction is made].
If it is argued that since a point must be established, and because it is stated again and again, repetition constitutes a point of defeat (*nigraha*), we say no.
Because the witnesses must be addressed with effort, because a fault is declared if they are not so addressed,
and because those to be addressed are the disciples.
Because it is a refutation of the debate of one seeking victory,
because of the rule of stating [a point] three times, and because of the repetition—

Furthermore, because there is no restriction regarding the convention [of usage] in the case of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), and since this does not differ from "excess" (*adhika*), it need not be mentioned separately. For when a word is employed that is already restricted [as being superfluous] in a proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*), it constitutes the fault of excess; thus, [the same applies] to its restatement.
Furthermore, even for a word whose meaning has already been understood, there is indeed a redundancy;
this applies even in discursive discussion (*prapañca-kathā*) where, although the subject matter consists of a single unmentioned means of accomplishment,
there is a desire to establish various meanings, or a desire to employ various means of accomplishment.

Since there is no fault in repeating for the sake of a listener who requires a multiplicity of reasons and so forth— because of the absence of conviction through what has already been understood— a multiplicity of reasons and a multiplicity of statements constitute a fault of the proof; thus,
this summary [shows] that redundancy (*ādhikya*) and repetition (*punarvacana*) share the same fault.
The statement is logical because,
due to the absence of defects, there is likewise an absence of [superior] qualities among such things.
And it has been stated that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the verbal expression of the various distinctions.

For another reason is the conceptualization of synonymous terms (*paryāya-śabda*); since these function with respect to an object already established by a single cause, there is no distinction for the person being informed. Furthermore, the meaning is—
Because it is being established [as such], it does not differ. Furthermore, as for what was said—
that in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is no tautology because of the repetition of words— [that is so].
Because a specific meaning is established,
just as the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the statement of the reason (*hetu*).
The statement of the very thesis itself, whose meaning is already understood, is a repetition; what, then, is its repetition?
Thus, the conclusion is improper.
Non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is the failure to restate that which has been understood by the assembly after it has been stated three times.
[This occurs] when the meaning of the statement has been understood by the assembly and by the opponent.
The failure to restate what has been stated three times is the point of defeat called "non-reproduction" (ananubhāṣaṇa). If one does not restate it, on what basis could one—

If it is argued that "one should effect the refutation of the thesis," and that this is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because the matter is concluded by the subsequent reply— that is to say,
through a reply characterized by merit or defect, one's state of being either deluded or undeluded is discerned— then [we respond as follows].

But what of one who has merely uttered [the response]? For there may be someone capable of providing an answer but not of repeating [the opponent's argument]; would such a person deserve defeat on that account? No, because he lacks full comprehension of the subject matter of the answer. If he does not repeat it...
The reply would result in being without an object. If, on the other hand, one offers a reply, how is it that one does not utter it? Thus, this which is said is contradictory:
"one does not utter [it]."
And he states the rejoinder. Furthermore, because it is not so asserted:
it is not asserted that everything must be uttered first, and the rejoinder only afterwards.
It must be stated;
however, some kind of answer must be given, and an answer is untenable in the absence of a basis.
It is correct that non-reiteration is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Even if the proponent, under the guise of explaining the meaning of his own proof, [introduces] by way of a consequence...

One should cause others to state one point after another; having stated merely the matter that is the subject of dispute and which is desired to be known, one should [proceed] through a succession of specific details regarding the meaning within the propositions and so forth.
Having introduced the subject matters, one should expand upon the discourse;
and when one is unable to recite all of that, [one should employ mnemonic verses].

What impairment of capacity is there in his stating merely the answer to the subject matter of that debate, by which [the opponent's] failure to repeat the proponent's statement would constitute a point of defeat?

A point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is thus defined. Therefore, one who fails to repeat the entire speech of the proponent is not incapable of providing a reply. For instance, the establishment of the object of inquiry is inseparable from the statement [of the reason], such as its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

In that case as well, there is merely the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and no further incidental argument (*prasaṅga*) is introduced; rather, because it necessarily concerns a component of the proof (*sādhana-aṅga*), it must indeed be demonstrated by means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). Even in that instance, not everything must be uttered in its prior sequence.

The refutation should be stated later, because of the undesirable consequence of having to utter [the argument] twice. Furthermore, if the restatement is intended merely to indicate the object of the refutation, then the proclamation of the sequence of the proponent's words is useless.

By one who refutes the effect itself, saying "this is its fault," a demonstration of the object is indeed made for every statement of a counter-fault because of its necessary connection (*nāntarīyatva*). For it is not possible to demonstrate all objects and [then] [refute them] simultaneously.
A fault cannot be stated [in general], because the faults differ according to each respective object. Therefore,
one must state the fault regarding whichever specific category of object it refutes.
At that time, that very [subject] which is the object of the refutation must be demonstrated, and not another;
for it is impossible to demonstrate another when one intends to refute that [specific subject].
When that [point] has been refuted, another point becomes the object of a further refutation;

this is the rule regarding both restatement and refutation. Even when there is a single restatement of everything at once, the subject must still be demonstrated at the time of stating the refutation.

Because it is impossible to state a fault when [the argument] has not been displayed, a double repetition would thus occur. In that case, the initial repetition of the entire sequence would be purposeless.
When a proponent of refutation must state a refutation, the utterance of that which is not applicable therein—
namely, the pointing out of what is not a fault and the repetition of what has already been said—
should be declared a ground for defeat consisting in the failure to restate everything once.
If it is argued, "Let it be so," this might be the case; however,
it has already been stated that [proving] a different matter constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Thus, in that context, if within a proof one states something that is not invariably concomitant (*anāntarīyaka*) by means of some incidental consequence (*prasaṅga*) or the like, this is indeed for the proponent a "deviation to another matter" (*arthāntara*);
he is therefore deserving of defeat. No incidental consequence whatsoever stated or produced therein [is valid].
It does not follow [that this fault applies]. Nor is that [objection] to be repeated by him,
nor is this even permitted by us.
Everything should be stated first all at once, and the refutation afterwards; however,
one who refutes must necessarily demonstrate the object [of that refutation].
"Otherwise, there would be no occurrence of a refutation.
If that is the case, then non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) should not be stated as a separate ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*),
because it is already included within "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*).

For non-comprehension of the reply is indeed *apratibhā*. And one who does not demonstrate the object of the reply is not capable of comprehending the reply; for there is no comprehension of a reply that is not implied by [the demonstration of] its object.

Non-reproduction [of the opponent's argument]. Since non-reproduction is pervaded by "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*), the status of being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) established for the latter is necessarily obtained for the former as well;
just as the possession of a dewlap and so forth, though established in a cow, is also present in a *bāhuleya* (a specific type of ox). Therefore...
Only *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity) should be stated as the ground for defeat,
not *ananubhāṣaṇa* (failure to repeat).
And what is this rule of convention that "failure to repeat [the opponent's argument] occurs when it has been stated three times"?
Thus [it is said]. If, first of all, the activity is for the purpose of instructing another, why should it be stated three times? He should be made to grasp it in such a way that he understands it.
It occurs. Now, if it is for the purpose of harming others,
then why is it recited three times?
Having whispered into the ears of the witnesses, the defendant should be harassed with difficult, well-known, rapid, or concise [questions],
so that he is unable to provide a reply.

The deluded person remains silent. Indeed, there is no principle whatsoever in the process of harming others by which [faults such as] the employment of harsh words, poorly understood expressions, or rapid pronunciation are prevented, nor is the requirement of stating [the question] three times enjoined. Furthermore, virtuous people do not engage in activities for the purpose of harming others.
Or rather, it must be said that treatises are composed; therefore,
it must first be stated [that he has not grasped them] as long as he has not understood them.

It is not only three times. One who is incapable of grasping [the meaning] must be refuted even before that, by means of one whose capacity has already been determined, after having awakened the opponent.
And "not understood" means ignorance. That which is not understood by the assembly or by the opponent, even though it has been stated, is called the point of defeat known as "ignorance.
For indeed, when the meaning is not understood, one cannot state its refutation.

This too, like non-reproduction, is not to be mentioned separately because it is understood through lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*) itself. Just as in the case of non-reproduction, since the subject matter has not been demonstrated, it is impossible to formulate a reply; thus, its status as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) follows simply from the failure to provide a reply.
Because repetition would be useless without the context of demonstrating the subsequent point,
even if such knowledge [of the point] exists, it results precisely from the failure to understand the answer.
Since one who does not know that [the opponent's statement] constitutes a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) could not possibly state a reply, nor the subject matter of the reply,
the knowledge of the subject matter is the knowledge of the reply.

And this is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because otherwise there would be no object for "lack of comprehension" (*anyathā-pratibhā*). For one who has not ascertained the meaning would not repeat it; and not repeating it, [one cannot state] the subject matter.
One would not be able to respond without having demonstrated the answer; thus, one might fail to provide a response.

However, this is impossible for one who knows the answer and its object, since it is impossible for such a person not to provide a response. Both of these [conditions] are causes for the failure to provide a response.
Since comprehension certainly occurs even in the absence of those two, one must state what the object of *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity) is when it is mentioned separately from them;
because it lacks an object, it is not to be spoken of.
It would be so.

It is not the lack of knowledge regarding the answer that constitutes *ajñāna* (ignorance); rather, it is the lack of knowledge regarding the subject matter (*viṣaya*). For if the subject matter is unknown, one cannot understand [the argument] due to the lack of knowledge regarding the answer; thus, the subject matter exists as the basis for *apratibhā* (inability to respond).

If this is argued, then, in that case, non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) would be without a distinct object, because it is subsumed under ignorance (*ajñāna*). For no one who correctly understands the subject matter would fail to reproduce it; thus, non-reproduction should not be stated as a separate point of defeat.

And because the ignorance of the answer is implied by the ignorance of the subject matter. Since one who does not know the subject matter cannot know the answer, the ignorance of the subject matter necessarily implies the ignorance of the answer as well; thus, there is no such thing as a "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*) that lacks a subject matter.

If it is argued that even when the subject matter is known, the subsequent lack of knowledge regarding the answer constitutes the scope of *apratibhā* (inability to respond), then in that case, further distinct points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) must be stated for both the lack of knowledge regarding the subject matter and the lack of knowledge regarding the answer. For example, just as there is "lack of knowledge regarding the subject matter" for *ajñāna*, there is likewise [a lack of knowledge regarding the answer].

Due to the distinction between "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) and so forth, even when there is no excellence of quality (*guṇātiśaya*), a separate determination of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is established;
likewise, even between two types of ignorance, [the distinction is made] between total ignorance and partial ignorance.

Why are other points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), such as the various subdivisions beginning with "ignorance" (*ajñāna*), not mentioned? Furthermore, there is no fault whatsoever in stating a summary that includes both types of ignorance; rather, there would even be an advantage. Therefore, a summary statement is logical.

Therefore, since non-reproduction and lack of comprehension are already included within the scope of *apratibhā* (inability to respond), they are not mentioned separately. Furthermore, there is no other ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) logically possible for either the proponent or the opponent apart from fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and *apratibhā*; thus, both [of these]—

"Everything has been stated by the mere statement itself. Since the various subdivisions implied by those two [categories] would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding speech and so forth in the absence of any excellence of quality (*guṇātiśaya*), such detailed elaboration (*prapañca*) is useless.
Non-reproduction of the response is "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*). When one does not produce a response that refutes the opponent's position, then one should be declared defeated.
Immediately after the statement of the proof (*sādhana*), it is unreasonable for one to waste time with respect to each point by means of subsequent rejoinders (*uttara*)—
such as proclaiming ignorance of that [proof], reciting verses, or the like—
and thus deserve defeat due to the failure to comprehend what ought to be done; this is a logical point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Thus:
*vikṣepa* (distraction) is the interruption of the discussion due to preoccupation with some other task; that is, one interrupts the discussion by claiming to have some other duty to perform.
"This duty of mine is being neglected; once this is finished, I shall attend to it afterwards."
When one interrupts the discourse with such remarks as, "My throat is afflicted by a cold," that is the point of defeat called *vikṣepa* (evasion),
since the discourse must conclude with the defeat of one of the two parties.
"He reaches the conclusion of the discussion by himself.
Even this, if the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) were to do so merely as a pretext for introducing a diversion,
and not because of an actual occurrence that would obstruct such a discussion—

If [the reason] exists, there would be a diversion (*vikṣepa*) precisely because of the determination that it lacks the capacity to establish its own [probandum]. And thus, this would be included within "shifting to another matter" (*arthāntara*) or among the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), due to the statement of a means of proof that is incapable. Regarding the subject at hand—

Furthermore, because it is a comprehension that is not connected to the proof (*sādhana*), it does not differ from the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) and the "incoherent" (*apārthaka*). Moreover, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if such distinct types of comprehension of unconnected proof-statements were to be treated as separate points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

This has been stated regarding the establishment [of the categories]. Now, if the proponent of the counter-position (*uttarapakṣavādī*) should thus engage in diversion (*vikṣepa*), then since the rejoinder (*uttara*) must be formulated immediately after the proof (*sādhana*), his failure to formulate it— his recognition of diversion—
is included either within "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*) or within "the irrelevant matter" (*arthāntara*).

Now, it is not necessarily the case that everything is understood solely through proof and refutation, such that every incorrect understanding on the part of the proponent and the opponent would have to be included either among fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) or among lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*). For indeed, [understanding] occurs even by means of what is unestablished.
If it is argued that there is dispute (*vivāda*) due to the proliferation of talk (*kathā-prapañca*), we say no, because it is impossible.
Dispute would occur between two contradictory assertions regarding a single locus (*adhikaraṇa*); [it cannot occur] between non-contradictory [assertions].

Because there can be no dispute between two parties who both accept [a position] or both do not accept it. In that case, one must necessarily speak first; for if they were to speak simultaneously, [dispute would be impossible].

Because it is impossible for there to be hearing, comprehension, and responses to one another's words, activity would be futile; thus, those who are composed in themselves do not engage [in debate]. Therefore, when presenting one's own position, a proof (*sādhana*) must necessarily be stated.
Otherwise, because others would not understand [the argument],
another person would offer a refutation based on that [misunderstanding].
When both parties have an incorrect understanding, there is the fallacy of the pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*) and the lack of rejoinder (*apratibhā*).

Regarding the term "consequence" (*prasaṅga*): every formal debate proceeding according to the rules of logic consists of the presentation of a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and a reply (*uttarapakṣa*), and does not exceed these two. By this very [definition], the *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is refuted, because in the absence of any accepted thesis, there can be no debate.
But when, having accepted the debate, one says nothing at all because of futility,
or prattles on about something else entirely, how then can that be a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)?
This is included [in the definition of defeat]. It has been stated that this refers specifically to the statement of an unestablished proof;

however, it has also been stated that defeat occurs in the case of both non-statement and the statement of something else, because one fails to state a member of the proof after having accepted the debate. By this, the redundant [is also explained].
Furthermore, the status of repetition and of stating the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth as points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has already been explained;
for these too result in the reversal of the matter to be established.

The failure to state the capacity of the proof (*sādhana*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because it is defined as the statement of a non-member of the proof due to the lack of comprehension of the means of cognition. Thus [it is said].
06113 *Matānujñā* (Admission of the Opponent's Position) is the attribution of a fault to the opponent's position by accepting that same fault for one's own position.
06114 When one, without having removed a fault pointed out by the opponent, says, "This fault belongs to you as well," [that is *matānujñā*].
For example, when it is said, "You are a thief because you are a human being," he might reply to that, "So are you."

Because he admits a fault in his own position and thereby attributes that same fault to the opponent's position, he accords with the opponent's view; thus, "accoring with the opponent's view" (matānujñā) is a point of defeat.
In this case as well, if you were a thief simply because of being a human being,
you would not have accepted such a self for yourself.
Therefore, if the intention is that this is not a cause for theft,
then there is no fault whatsoever.

And why is it not [considered] a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) directly, rather than through a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), by pointing out the defect in that very [subject] which is not intended [as the locus], namely, by showing the presence of the reason (*hetu*) as being like a thief?
If you say, "This is of little consequence, for such worldly conventions do indeed exist," then even if one accepts that proposal, [the following applies]:
He is subject to defeat solely because of his failure to provide a response to that proof,
not because of the introduction of his own fault elsewhere.

For, if the means of proof for that [thesis] is indeed faultless, then the opponent's mere admission of it constitutes a failure to provide a response; since, by that much alone, the opponent has already incurred defeat,
any subsequent raising of faults against him is irrelevant.

Neglecting one who deserves censure is the failure to press for a point of defeat when one has reached it. One who "deserves censure" (paryanuyojya) is one who should be urged [to respond] because a ground for defeat has arisen;
neglecting such a person is [the fault].
"You have been defeated"— this is not a formal rejoinder. Furthermore, this must be stated by the assembly when asked, "Whose defeat is this?",
for one who has been defeated does not [himself] declare it.
"One should expose one's own private parts.
Even in this case, if the respondent does not interrogate the proponent who has fallen into a state of defeat, [the debate remains incomplete].

Since "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*) is simply the failure to provide a response, "neglecting the one who should be questioned" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) is not a separate ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Furthermore, in the investigation of logic (*nyāyacintā*), there can be neither victory nor defeat for either of the two parties here, because of the [failure of the] proof—
Because [the opponent] does not establish the meaning through the appearance [of the argument], and because they do not state the actual fault. Furthermore,
if they point out some fault but not another, then at that time—
[The opponent argues: "He deserves defeat because he fails to provide a reply.

[The proponent replies: "He certainly does deserve it, because he fails to point out every existing fault. [The opponent says: "No; for if they exist, all faults must necessarily be stated, or else [if they are not stated,]"...
There is refutation [of the opponent's position] because even by a single [means] there is an obstruction to that proof,
just like the statement of a single means of proof.
For example, even when many means of proof exist for a single object, [the goal is achieved] by one alone.

Since that [point] is established, it is not the case that everything must be stated as the material cause; thus, one who merely fails to point out a fault in another is liable for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Now, suppose the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) [recognizes that] the proponent of the rejoinder (*uttarapakṣavādī*) has reached a state of defeat.
If he does not refute it, then, according to the rule, neither of the two has victory or defeat as before. [He should] [refute] the respondent who states a fallacy (*doṣābhāsa*). His own...
If one does not remove [the opponent's position] through a proof, there is no victory for the proponent because he has failed to establish the members of his proof;

for he must establish the members of the proof by demonstrating the impossibility of all possible faults. Nor is there victory for the respondent, because he has failed to point out an actual fault. Therefore...
Even so, "ignoring" (upekṣaṇa) that which is not subject to censure is not a ground for defeat (parājaya-adhikaraṇa).
To urge a ground of defeat (nigrahasthāna) at an inappropriate time is "censuring one who is not to be censured" (niranuyojya-anuyoga). [This is] a ground of defeat.

If, by making a false determination regarding the definition [of a point], one says "you have been defeated" when you have not actually been defeated, you should be declared defeated for "reproaching what is not to be reproached.
In this case as well, if one [accuses] the proponent of that proof with non-existent faults in the reply—
If one should charge another with a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) when it is misplaced and faultless, that person is not one who points out a ground for defeat;
for such a case lacks the defining characteristic of pointing out an actual fault.

Since the opponent is unable to provide a reply, and it has been demonstrated by the other party that his response is a fallacious rejoinder (*uttarābhāsa*), he is defeated by *apratibhā* (inability to respond) itself; therefore, this is not a separate ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Now, [consider] the respondent who points out an actual defect in the proof (*sādhana*)...
If another person should attack with a statement that appears to be a fallacy (doṣābhāsa),
and once its status as a real fallacy has been established by him, [the opponent] is defeated solely by means of that statement which appeared to be a fallacious proof (sādhanābhāsa).

Even so, this does not differ from the fallacies of the reason (*hetv-ābhāsa*). For the fallacies of the reason must necessarily be stated as points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in order to pervade other objects;
once they have been stated, the statement of anything else is redundant.
Deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*) is the consequence of a debate due to a lack of restriction after having accepted a tenet.
Having asserted that a certain matter exists in a particular way,
to engage in a debate by reversing the meaning of what was asserted constitutes deviation from a tenet.
It should be understood as follows: having accepted the established tenet that "there is no destruction of what exists,
nor does what does not exist arise," one posits a thesis [such as] "there is a single primordial nature."

Because modifications of the manifest are seen to have a common underlying continuity (*anvaya*). For instance, it is observed that bowls and other such objects, which possess the continuity of clay, originate from a single material cause;
and so too is this manifest [world].

A particular modification is perceived as being endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion; therefore, it is said that [the world] has a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of pleasure and the rest. Having been told this, he is questioned:
"Now, how is 'primordial nature' and 'modification' (*vikāra*) to be defined? [It is that] which remains constant...
When one property ceases, another property arises;
that is the *prakṛti* (primordial nature). That which is the other property is the *vikāra* (modification). This is it.
Because it contradicts the subject matter under discussion and lacks necessity, he introduces an irrelevant argument. For he has indeed asserted that "the non-existent does not come into being,
nor does the existent disappear."

Furthermore, since for anyone there can be neither the cessation of activity nor the engagement in activity without the concealment and manifestation of the existent and the non-existent, if one who has thus been challenged should admit the self-destruction of the existent and the self-acquisition of the non-existent;
If he does not accept [the consequence], it becomes a departure from his own tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and thus his thesis is not established.
In this case as well, there is no occasion for debate due to any lack of restriction,
because he has accepted that what is non-existent does not arise and what is existent does not perish; [this is stated] for the sake of establishing that.
This has been stated: "This manifest world has a single primordial nature (prakṛti), because its commonality is observed.

In this context, the single primordial nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion. This manifest world has that as its undifferentiated source, because its commonality with that [nature] is observed. Of the manifest...

Because their identity with that [pleasure, etc. is observed to be distinct—since pleasure and the rest are not admitted to have arising and destruction—it is established that for everything of that nature, there is no arising and no destruction. Herein lies the fault of the reason stated by him.

Without having pointed out the characteristics of modification (*vikāra*) and primordial matter (*prakṛti*), he himself initiates the discussion by asking questions unrelated to the subject at hand, proceeding without restraint.
In that case, this should be said:
The manifest (vyakta) is characterized by the properties of activity and cessation,
whereas pleasure and the like are not so. If the manifest were associated with pleasure and the like,
then its very nature would consist of pleasure and so forth, and it would consequently lose its defining characteristic of having the properties of activity and cessation.

"It is being excluded. Since the concomitance of pleasure and so forth is observed, the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha).
In this way, by pointing out a flaw in his proof, his thesis (pakṣa) is refuted.
It happens that, without having addressed the fault in the proof (*sādhana*), he prolongs the discussion and projects his own fault onto the other.
If it is argued that "this very fault is what is being stated by means of this context," [the response follows].
This is the domain of those who rely on omens;
the world is not capable of understanding a meaning that has not been communicated by words. This very point follows the analogy of the "painting of a buffoon."

In this case as well, according to the principle already stated, defeat occurs precisely because of the statement of a previously mentioned reason that lacks a constituent of proof (*asādhana-aṅga*) or is unestablished (*asiddha*),
and not because of a lack of restriction.
Regarding the phrase "due to the context of the discussion": this too need not be mentioned separately, as it is included among the fallacies of the reason (*hetv-ābhāsa*).
And the fallacies of the reason have been explained as they were; furthermore, the fallacies of the reason are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Furthermore, do fallacious reasons (*hetv-ābhāsa*) become points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) by virtue of being associated with a different characteristic,
just as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [become] objects of cognition (*prameya*)?
Therefore, he says: "The state of being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs precisely through the characteristics of the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) as previously described.
Here too, one must reflect by applying the same principle as stated before.

Are these [fallacies] exactly as they were characterized by their divisions, or are they otherwise? Since that [question], when considered here, would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), it is not elaborated upon. And the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are [to be understood] according to the proper method.
"Points of defeat" (nigrahasthāna)— this much alone is intended.

This *Vādanyāya*, which scrapes away the cataracts of the darkness of ignorance from the world and provides the vision of reality, has been composed by the virtuous who delight in the welfare of others.
This person of poor discernment darkens that light of reality; therefore, I have made this effort here to illuminate it. (3)
